maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. FISHER-COLLUSION IN PREPARATION OF QUESTIONS FOR ORDER PAPER-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Order. I should like to deal with a matter raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) some few days ago. As reported at page 11963 of Hansard of March 4 last the hon. member for Port Arthur stated:
I wish to raise a question of privilege which appears to involve collusion between officials of the Department of Justice and certain members of parliament, in particular Messrs. Francis, Bas-ford and Macaluso. To illustrate this collusion I should like to make reference to certain questions on the order paper, being questions Nos. 2,042, 2,608, 2,766 and 2,805.
Subsequently in his remarks the hon. member for Port Arthur also said:
It is my belief that when you, sir, and other members of this house read these questions to which I have made reference you will wonder why they were ever accepted. The rules indicate that questions should be framed in such a way as to elicit information rather than give it. These questions appear to me to transgress many of the rules we have in respect of the kind of questions which should be allowed.
It seems to me that there are two aspects of the question raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur. On the one hand there is the allegation that there was collusion between certain hon. members and officials of the Department of Justice, and on the other that certain questions were irregular as to form and content.
Having stated the alleged question of privilege raised by the hon. member objectively and fairly-at least I hope so-may I now say that the Speaker's responsibility with regard to questions as stated at page 355 of May's sixteenth edition, "is limited to their compliance with the rules of the house. Responsibility in other respects rests with the member who proposes to ask the question".
That is the end of that quotation. I am also prepared to say that the rules and conventions with respect to questions are being applied in much the same manner now as they have
been applied under at least two of my predecessors. I would suggest it is neither feasible, necessary nor desirable for the Chair or the clerks at the table to look in behind the terminology of a question for the purpose of ascertaining whether a question is inspired, so to speak, or whether it is being put on the paper for the purpose of embarrassing or harassing a member or members of this house.
May I also add that I am not sure that it is irregular, immoral or contrary to usages for an hon. member to obtain information from a department either by a telephone call, through correspondence or by a personal visit to a department, and having obtained such information place questions on the order paper based upon or using therein some of the information so obtained. From a procedural point of view I am unable to find any authority or support for that proposition.
Therefore, for the reasons stated, it is my duty to say that I am unable to find that a prima facie question of privilege arises from the wording of the questions to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred in his remarks on Thursday, March 4 last; and in consequence I cannot accept the motion presented at that time by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.
However, the question raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur went deeper than procedure, when he went on to say the following, as reported at page 11963 of Hansard for March 4 last:
I think all members of parliament, whether government or opposition, only ask for a fair chance. After consultation with your officials, Mr. Speaker, who deal with the order paper and questions of procedure, I now put before you for your advice the question whether there is a clearcut case here of collusion of the kind that would attack the traditional parliamentary rights of members of parliament.
Having given much study to the wording of the questions enumerated by the hon. member for Port Arthur, the Chair is unable to find any grounds to establish the fact that there has been a clear cut case of collusion between certain hon. members and officials of the Department of Justice or any other department of the kind which would attack the traditional parliamentary rights of mem-

Question of Privilege
bers of parliament. It seems to me that a clearcut charge of this nature would be a fitting and proper question for reference to the standing committee on privileges and elections, and if such were made the Chair would be prepared to accept a motion setting out a definite charge of this nature in which any member or members who may be involved or implicated therein are named.
In this regard I might reiterate in part a statement by the Chair made on Friday, October 30, 1964, as reported at page 9595 of Hansard. At that time I said:
It is undoubtedly a very serious thing to attack the conduct of any member of the House of Commons, and in that respect a specific charge should always be made, not a general charge. I am confirmed in this opinion by an excellent ruling, it seems to me, given by Mr. Speaker Michener on June 19, 1959, which appears on pages 583 and 584 of the Journals. I should like to refer to two short sentences in that ruling. I read from page 583:
"It has been strongly urged by some members that the house should not set in motion its power to try and to judge the conduct of a member unless such member is charged with a specific offence. It is urged further that not only must he be charged, but that he must be charged by a member of the House of Commons standing in his place."
I will now deal, if I may, with the form and the content of the eight questions referred to by the hon. member for Port Arthur in his remarks on March 4 last. With reference to questions 2,720 to 2,724 inclusive, I can find nothing unique or unusual in the wording of these questions. It is not possible for the Chair or for officers of the house to determine whether or not they were placed on the order paper by way of harassment as suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur. In this regard I can do no better than to use the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre when, as reported at page 11964 of Hansard for March 4 last, he said:
Surely it is no function of the Speaker to ascertain whether or not access to files has been made available to private members of the house. I do not know what sort of investigation Mr. Speaker could carry on in that regard.
In my opinion, what I have said about questions numbered 2,720 to 2,724 inclusive will apply equally well to questions numbered 2,608, 2,766 and 2,805.
I now come to question No. 2,042, notice of which was filed on October 2, 1964, and which was read into the record and referred to specifically by the hon. member for Port Arthur on March 4 last in the following words:
Mr. Speaker, it is apparent from the information contained in that question that it is ex-

tremely unlikely the hon. member for Carleton had the specified dates and facts at his fingertips.
It is not my intention to quibble about the form or substance of this question, but I am of the opinion that it might have been drafted in terms more general in nature than those which were used. However, in fairness I should point out that much has been said in a report by a commissioner of inquiry which was laid before the house, in the courts of this country, in the newspapers of this land, and indeed in the debates in this house as well, concerning the Hal Banks case. Personally I was of the opinion that almost every facet of that question was of public knowledge.
It may be of interest to the house, I think, if I were to quote at this time an eminent and widely recognized authority on parliamentary procedure, Sir Gilbert Campion, a long time clerk of the British House of Commons, at page 145 of his "Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons", 1946 edition, where he states in part as follows:
Not later than three o'clock the question hour begins. This is a more important item of business than any yet described. It is expected to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions "turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service". Their chief object is "the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events", and "they are often arranged by the government itself so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way". They are "serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers". And finally "questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity".
"Most of these authorities agree also that the privilege of asking questions is liable to abuse and that the number of questions has increased inordinately."
It is apparent that what was true in the British house in 1946 is also applicable in this house today. To emphasize this point I need only refer to the more than 3,000 questions which have appeared on the order paper during this session alone.
I have referred to Campion only for the purpose of indicating that it is time this house took a long and hard look at the machinery and the rules of procedure covering the asking of questions. The purposes for which questions are now asked have altered considerably since standing order 39(1) was enacted in 1867, but apparently the terms of this standing order and the machinery followed

in handling questions have remained unaltered for almost a century. For example, one need only look at citation 171 of Beau-chesne's fourth edition in which will be found numerous and, in many cases, inoperable restrictions covering the form and content of questions. I suggest that if each and every one of these restrictions were applied in every case, very few questions would ever reach the order paper.
I regret having taken up so much time of the house at this time, but I propose, if the house will agree, to have this entire question studied by the special committee on procedure and organization in order to have the machinery covering the handling of questions modernized and to have rules laid down which will serve the purposes of and assist hon. members in posing questions.
In conclusion I should like to thank the hon. member for Port Arthur for having raised this question, since it may cause the special committee on procedure and organization to focus its full attention on a long neglected but important part of the procedure of this house.

speechtext:
May I also take this opportunity to discuss two questions raised by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), and this will be considerably shorter.
On Friday, March 12, 1965 the hon. member for Danforth asked two questions of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Nicholson), the first as follows:
I wonder what steps the minister is taking to investigate the circumstances under which Senator Gelinas was supplied confidential information from the files of the department by Raymond Denis in the Stonehill case, as reported in the press.
The second question was:
Is the minister aware that Raymond Denis has given testimony under oath to the effect that information from the files of his department was made available to Senator Gelinas?
Objection was taken to these questions. To the first question I made the objection that it contained an assertion, an allegation. To the two questions the Minister of Transport objected that they were questions about proceedings before a royal commission which is sitting at this time.
The hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam were of the opinion that this particular evidence in
Grain Payments
no way involved a matter that was sub judice, and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam added:
I believe Your Honour will want to take under advisement the question as to whether evidence given before the Dorion commission which is not related to the terms of reference under which that commission is operating can be the subject of questions asked in this house. The particular question raised by the hon. member for Danforth related to the Stonehill case, and nowhere under the terms of reference is Mr. Justice Dorion authorized to investigate the Stonehill case...
May in his seventeenth edition at page 352 gives examples of inadmissible questions and, as set out in subparagraph 8, among the types of question ruled out of order are those dealing with matters referred to a royal commission. It would seem to me that the Stonehill case, not having been referred to the Dorion commission, does not fall within the terms of reference under which the commission is operating and therefore is in no way sub judice.
However, it would appear that these questions should not have been asked in their present form, and I do not think they would be proper questions to be put on the order paper as they now read. As I mentioned when the first question was asked in the house by the hon. member for Danforth, it is in the nature of an assertion or an allegation. I have come to the view that such questions should not be allowed in their present form, but I see no serious objection to having them put on the order paper if drafted in proper form.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view

Citizenship Policy
of the important principle involved in the Bergsma case and of the question asked a few days ago in the house by the hon. member for Hamilton South, I should like to make a short statement on the government's intentions with respect to Mr. and Mrs. Bergsma, the couple who were recently refused citizenship by a judge of the citizenship court, His Honour Judge Leach.
Hon. members are aware that, on March 17, Mr. Justice Schatz of the high court of Ontario pronounced a judgment confirming the decision of the citizenship court judge. My immediate predecessor in office and the Minister of Justice, and more recently my parliamentary secretary, have told the house of the government's concern over this particular case, and have predicted the introduction, if found necessary, of amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act with a view to correcting the situation.
With all due respect for the opinions of the two judges mentioned, both my department and I are concerned about the soundness of the original decision and the judgment of the high court confirming it. We had not thought that the citizenship act could be interpreted in the way it has now been interpreted. As a matter of fact I am informed that several citizenship court judges have permitted applicants to affirm rather than require them to swear the oath of allegiance.
The Attorney General of Canada feels that the legal question involved should be settled by a court of final resort. It seems less than reasonable that Mr. and Mrs. Bergsma should be required to bear the legal costs of contesting a decision on an aspect of the legislation with which the government is not in agreement and which, if sustained, we intend to ask parliament to change. I am sure, therefore, that hon. members will be pleased to learn that the crown intends to pay the reasonable costs to Mr. and Mrs. Bergsma of pursuing this matter in the courts; and their legal adviser, Mr. Ian G. Scott of Toronto, is being or has been advised accordingly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: NEWFOUNDLAND-AGREEMENT ON FINANCING OF CONSTRUCTION OF TRANSMISSION FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the northern Canada power commission has today concluded an agreement with the Newfoundland and Labrador power commission under the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, to finance the construction of power transmission facilities in connection with Newfoundland's Bay d'Espoir hydroelectric project at a cost of about $17,700,000.
Under this agreement a transmission line system 320 miles long will be constructed in eastern and northwestern Newfoundland. The transmission line and facilities will serve such centres as St. John's on the Avalon peninsula and Corner Brook on the west coast. The Atlantic development board has already agreed to provide $24 million to help finance the construction of the power plant itself and to assist in the conversion to 60 cycle power of the electric services of central Newfoundland and the west coast.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-142, respecting the operation of certain established federal-provincial programs, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lambert.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the current debate I am sure many members on both sides of this house have become convinced of one important thing, namely that our constitution itself should be a modern constitution suited to modern times. It is my impression that many members in all corners of the house have been convinced of that fact, and I might say that I intend to relate my remarks to the amendment.
I do not say this in a partisan sense, but it is my impression that the government should have set up machinery a long time ago in order that we might have obtained agreement that our constitution should be modern and suited to modern times. This could be brought about by a series of federal-provincial conferences held at different times in different parts of the country. I do not suggest that we repeat the performance that took place before 1867, when in order to get confederation and this nation on the

Dominion-Provincial Relations rails in the first place we actually had a Liberal-Conservative coalition. I am suggesting, however, that the federal government should take the initiative, certainly before it places this kind of detailed legislation before this house in relation to federal-provincial relations, to set up an all-party committee to study our constitution. Members of parliament and members of the Senate could be appointed to this committee.
One of the first tasks of this committee would be to travel from one end of Canada to the other conferring with similar bodies if possible or with the governments of the day in the provincial capitals. The next step would be to meet in Ottawa, where findings could be made by the committee and further studies carried out. A final meeting would then follow of the federal and provincial committees.
Let me say at the outset that the results of such a series of conferences might indicate one of three things; that the constitution should remain exactly as it is, because it is flexible enough for current needs; that it should be amended slightly, or that it should be entirely scrapped. I use the word "scrapped" advisedly although perhaps it is not the best word to use in this debate. My suggestion is based on the idea that there are generally speaking three points of view in this country today; one expressed by those who feel we need a new constitution, one expressed by those who feel the present constitution is sufficiently flexible for present needs, and another expressed by those who feel it needs only slight amendment.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, the government should have taken the initiative a long time ago to make sure these different points of view were brought to the conference table. Whatever might happen, we cannot expect miracles, but such a series of conferences would go a long way toward establishing agreement in respect of our constitution. Whatever the results of such a series of conferences, the resulting constitution I suggest would be a modern one suited to modern times. I plead with the government to take this kind of initiative before they, again, proceed with the type of detailed legislation we are currently considering.
Relating my remarks to the amendment at hand, surely if we have this type of a conference it will also mean that we can discuss priorities, and that is the kernel of our amendment. I plead with the government to take this kind of initiative before continuing

with this alternative type of ad hoc legislation in relation to federal-provincial problems.

We must realize that, while we wish to see some progress in the federal legislation concerning the Canadian economy, it is important that our federal-provincial relations be at their best. At this point, I wish to suggest something to the government, in all broadness of mind. When we are not in agreement with the policy advocated by this government concerning national unity, or federal-provincial relations, it is not enough to answer that we, the Conservatives, are anti-Quebec. On the contrary, I can assure you that we are of good faith.

I should like to repeat what I said. At the present time in this Canadian House of Commons we are beginning to seriously realize that we cannot make progress in many legislative fields which affect the economy of Canada unless we do everything possible in every corner of this house to improve national unity and federal-provincial relations in the truest sense of the word. I for one, and I think I speak for the majority of members in all parties, suggest that when we are dealing with this subject of federal-provincial relations in this year 1965 we must try to reach a bipartisan level.
On every occasion when we do not agree with the government in respect of questions of national unity, on every occasion when we suggest an alternative proposal, and on every occasion when we fail to say "Yes, yes, yes" to the government in respect of its measures designed to improve national unity and federal-provincial relations, I suggest it is not fitting for the government to reply by suggesting that the leader of this party and the members of this party are anti-Quebec. The Liberal party has been doing precisely that in the province of Quebec since 1867. It has been making this kind of smear there for many years, and I suggest that my people are now going to stop it. The answer to our propositions, which the government has continually given, that is that we are anti-Quebec, is no longer a good enough answer. Let me suggest immediately that while the current dialogue of debate is taking place, many people in the province of Quebec whose voices have not been heard are thinking that we must maintain a strong central government in Canada.

I should like to say right away, sir, that substantively speaking this legislation is correct. I have no argument with its general purport. With relation to most of the joint programs listed in the bill it is my view that the provinces have a perfect right, legally and in every other way, to opt out of these programs. But here in parliament we must be cognizant of what Haldane said about justice; that justice must not only be just, it must seem just. Like so many things this government has done, while this legislation substantively speaking may be correct, the timing of the government is bad. They have brought in legislation of this type at a time when they have failed for so long to do so many other things related to the central problem of federal-provincial relations.
As I proceed with my remarks I should like to discuss the proposed amendment to the bill and some principles of federal-provincial relations for which I for one feel our party stands. 1 should also like to discuss a few general things in the field of federal-provincial relations that I think the government should have done before they confronted the Canadian people and the Canadian House of Commons with the type of ad hoc, patchwork legislation with which we are faced today. Then I should like to close my remarks by, 1 hope, objectively criticizing the government's performance in general in the field of federal-provincial relations.
By way of introduction let me simply say that I do not think it is good enough just to say that because provincial premiers, even if those provincial premiers are Conservative, advocate a certain course of action this necessarily means that the federal Conservative party in the House of Commons must automatically agree. When provincial premiers, be they N.D.P., Social Credit, Conservative or Liberal, come to Ottawa to engage in federal-provincial conferences or for any other purpose they must defend the provincial cause no matter what their political stripe is. It has been ever thus since confederation. On the other hand federal parties, no matter what their political stripe may be and no matter at what period in the evolution of Canadian history they are acting, must defend the federal cause and powers. Because the Prime Minister at various times chooses to do otherwise I simply reiterate and emphasize the fact that this is his choice.
In the corridors of the House of Commons during the past week it has been said to me, for example, with regard to this legislation we are now discussing that it is impossible to disagree with it because revenue
Dominion-Provincial Relations minister Kierans of the province of Quebec has his tax forms already prepared based on the passage of legislation of this kind. In many ways I have great respect for the revenue minister of the province of Quebec, but I think this is a very dangerous attitude for federal political parties, be they in the opposition or in the government, to take. While we realize there has got to be give and take, compromise, understanding and good will and the ability to see both sides of the question in federal-provincial relations, when all is said and done the federal government must defend the federal cause, and people in every corner of Canada, including the province of Quebec, are very concerned lest we water down the strength of the federal government.
But do not misunderstand me, Mr. Speaker. I am not saying this particular piece of opting out legislation would do that. I have already said that I agree with it in substance, but in some respects one wonders why this legislation has been brought before us. Is it not merely crossing the t's and dotting the i's and only putting into legislative form that which I have always felt the provinces could do at any time? At any rate, if many people are perhaps regarding this legislation in a mistaken way, I say again it is because of the bad timing of the government and, as Haldane said, in this instance justice will not seem to have been done.
Before I proceed to review the government's performance in the field of federal-provincial relations I should like in discussing the amendment to refer to some principles with regard to federal-provincial relations which my party feels it is most important that we should adhere to at this time.

It must be realized that the constitution of Canada-and I want to repeat this as often as possible-is the first in the world to combine a federal government system with a parliamentary system.
I always believed that a federal system of government should try and combine a measure of unity with a measure of diversity.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that Canada never was and never will be united along the lines of the principle of the melting pot. Everyone knows that we have a small population spread over a vast territory, and I believe that when our population is much larger, when means of communication are faster than ever, our motto toward Canada should be: Unity in diversity.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Our federalism is based on a particular psychology among the various people and provinces, a psychology which results in a desire for union, but not for unity of language, culture, religion and so forth.
Such a stand for unity in diversity should always be considered as a positive and dynamic factor in our national make-up. The truth is that this basic diversity in our national life often gives rise to numerous problems through the years of our nation's development. We are faced with some of those problems at the present time. I think that, when we are content to speak of the need for mutual respect and understanding and the need for co-operation, we are not being positive enough, far from it, in taking this attitude of live and let live. It goes without saying that co-operation and understanding are essential elements of our attitude, but the sooner we concentrate on the positive advantages of our diversity, the less we shall be hearing about a confederation crisis. Then, we shall start looking outwards as well as inwards.

When we say that our party was the party of confederation-I am now enunciating some of our party's principles with relation to the amendment, the bill and federal-provincial relations-it has much greater significance than simply underlining the fact that we were in power in 1867. The spirit of Macdonald and Cartier means more than that. It means that we have two great founding races and Canadians of many cultural and ethnic origins working together to build our country.
This gives Canada its unique strength, and this spirit of unity in diversity keynotes the fact that the melting pot theory is not applicable to the Canadian mosaic. A Conservative believes a man can be intensely loyal to his family, to his church, to his community; and when he does this there is no reason to hold that his love of country has diminished. We recognize, sir, in this party, as so often the government does not, that people on the local level know what is best for them and how best to govern their own affairs.
I think to a great extent this principle is being underlined in the legislation before us which permits, at this time in our nation's history, those provinces who wish to do so to opt out of certain programs. I am told that the expression "opt out" is not all that desirable. Perhaps we can all get together and think of a more suitable expression which
[Mr. Grafftey.i
would not lend itself so often to misunderstanding.
Let me quote from two great men who understood Conservative principles, principles which I believe are applicable to the Canadian scene at this time, namely Salisbury and Burke. In my view these general observations illustrate the universality of Conservative principles, even in Canada in 1965. I think they should be underlined as we are considering the principles of the amendment and of the bill itself. The following is an excerpt from a speech by Lord Salisbury on the Conservative party at Newport on Monday, October 7, 1885, which illustrates the persistent Conservative advocacy of a more equitable balance of initiative and authority between central and local governments. He said;
Now bear in mind what true reform and local government means. It does not only mean-what I quite admit-that the local authorities should be popularly elected; hut it means that when you have got at what you want, when you have provided the proper constitution of local authority, you must provide that the local authority has sufficient powers, and that it gets those powers by diminishing the excessive and exaggerated powers which have been heaped on the central authorities in London.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me quote-pertinently, I believe-from a speech by Edmund Burke, because it illustrates the traditional Conservative attitude toward the morbid concentration of power in modern states, another principle upon which I think many supporters of the government would agree. I believe this is a principle that should be underlined at this time in Canada's evolution:
It is boasted that the geometrical policy has been adopted, that all local ideas should be sunk, and that the people should be no longer Gascons, Picards, Bretons, Normans; but Frenchmen, with one country, one heart and one assembly. But instead of being all Frenchmen, the greater likelihood is that the inhabitants of that region will shortly have no country. No man ever was attached by a sense of pride, partiality, or real affection to a description of square measurements. He never will glory in belonging to chequer number 71, or to any other badge-ticket. We begin our public affections in our families. No cold relation is a zealous citizen. We pass on to our neighbourhoods, and our habitual provincial connections. These are inns and resting places. Such divisions of our country as have been formed by habit, and not by a sudden jerk of authority, were so many images of the great country in which the heart found something which it could fill. The love of the whole is not extinguished by this subordinate partiality.
I should like to interject here, Mr. Speaker, a note which I think many members would agree with, and that is that because Quebeckers love their province it does not in any

way diminish their love for their country called Canada. Burke went on to say:
Perhaps it is a sort of elemental training to those higher and more large regards by which alone men come to be affected, as with their own concern, in the prosperity of a kingdom. To be attached to the subdivision, to love the little platoon we belong to in society, is the first principle (the germ, as it were) of our public affections. It is the first link in the series by which we proceed toward a love of our country, and of mankind.
Having said these things, I admit at some length, I fully recognize that on the other side of the coin the federal government was created in Canada to guarantee minimum social and economic conditions in every part of our country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. When we talk about provincial autonomy we should be equally aware of the fact that the federal position must be zealously guarded.
This is one lesson that I am not sure the present government has learned or understands. The federal government, too, has its autonomy. The Conservative will fight extremes wherever he finds them in Canada. The Conservative will fight the extreme of centralization. The Conservative will fight the extreme of decentralization. We therefore arrive at what somebody will call the obvious conclusion, that in Canada we must have a strong federal government acting in co-operation with strong provincial governments, both acting within their respective constitutional jurisdictions. This is almost axiomatic, Mr. Speaker. However, it is something that must be repeated time and time again.
What principles and considerations will help to bring about such a state of affairs? The principles and considerations that I am about to enunciate relate to federal-provincial relations and things which this government has neglected to get under way. They must get activity in these general areas under way as soon as possible. Permanent consultative machinery between Ottawa and the provinces must be improved immediately. A real secretariat for federal-provincial relations must be established at the heads of government level.
Now, Mr. Speaker, every time I mention this subject and say this is something that must be done before we act on this type of ad hoc, patchwork legislation, ministers opposite say such a secretariat has been set up in the privy council office under the right hon. Prime Minister, who reports directly to this house on federal-provincial relations. The type of secretariat about which I am 20220-819J
Dominion-Provincial Relations talking, the type of secretariat based on the ARDA approach and the natural resources approach so well understood by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he was minister of agriculture, is the type upon which we should base such a secretariat. I say this because in the field of ARDA, in the field of renewable resources, as many members recognize we have initiated real federal-provincial cooperation based on a secretariat of this kind. The secretariat which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) says has been set up in the privy council offices, with the help of one or two senior officials who are already overworked, is not the type of secretariat I have in mind.
The provinces and the federal government must meet as soon as possible to plan priorities. This must be done before patchwork legislation of the type we now have before us is brought before the Canadian House of Commons. If it is, even though, objectively speaking, the legislation may be in accordance with the strict terms of the law we shall be obliged once again to take a critical stand: It is the timing which is so important. It should not be forgotten that this government's greatest failure to date has taken place in the field of federal-provincial relations.
I may have my rose-coloured glasses on, but I think the old reactionary Tory who worried about the growth of government expenditure is a thing of the past. At least I hope he is. There is no longer any reason to fear the growth of governmental expenditure in itself. Big government is not necessarily a bad thing, provided we make sure that the state works for the individual and not the individual for the state. We recognize that more public institutions must be built- roads, parks, hospitals, improved prison institutions. All these things must be done. We have been talking about plans for medicare. Surely the government in a bipartisan way can accept a suggestion whether it comes from Premier Roblin or from any other premier, or indeed from any corner of this house. Surely the government can swallow its pride and get together with the provinces as quickly as possible in order to plan priorities.
There is a third thing which I believe needs to be done; I have listed it third but perhaps it should have come first on the list. As I indicated at the beginning of my remarks we should obtain agreement as quickly as possible so as to obtain a modern constitution suited to modern times. I have already suggested in brief outline a series of conferences

Dominion-Provincial Relations through which this goal could be attained. We should not expect miracles, but such meetings as these would go a long way toward alleviating the present situation. Certainly, before patchwork, ad hoc legislation such as this is brought forward for consideration by the House of Commons again, such a series of consultational conferences should be held. Why should we have such a series of conferences?

First, let us deal very briefly, Mr. Speaker, with the matter of public education.
How many times has it been said that almost a hundred years ago our economy was mostly a rural one. Education came under the provinces' jurisdiction. I will not give statistics but in 1867, at the time of the little red school house, expenditures for education were much lower than they are today. In this era of high automation, a good education is essential and our provinces must have the financial resources and sufficient taxation powers to fulfil their ever increasing responsibilities.

There is another reason why we should begin right away to hold a series of constitutional conferences so as to modernize our constitution. I have in mind the difficulties presently being faced by our cities, towns, municipalities and metropolitan areas. I fully admit-and I am not being patronizing in this sense-that according to the terms of our constitution cities, towns and metropolitan areas fall under the authority of the provinces by virtue of section 92. However, the sprawling metropolitan areas we find in Canada today are not cities and towns in the sense of those words in 1867 when our constitution was drawn up. We see a metropolitan area about to come into being in Montreal. One already exists in Ontario and others are planned to come into existence. Already we have metropolitan areas which prepare annual budgets larger than those of several of our provinces. While I freely admit that the provinces have the prior responsibility under the terms of the constitution with respect to this new form of metropolitan area, the federal government surely cannot turn its back on the problems which face these sprawling cities and metropolitan areas in 1965-problems involving urban renewal, parks, playgrounds, the treatment of the aged and the disabled, physical fitness, juvenile delinquency, and so on. Again, I maintain that the federal

government cannot turn its back on the difficulties confronting these new units of government in this modern day and age.
I find it hard to put into words the third consideration I have in mind-relating to why we should get this constitutional conference under way as soon as possible. Let me simply say this: At the time of confederation in 1867 there was a union in many ways between the two great founding races. Today, those speaking for the vast majority of French speaking Canadians say they want to remain in an outward looking and dynamic confederation. Without placing blame in any direction they simply state that up to the present they have not been equal partners on the national scene. Common sense adjustments must be made in a spirit of good will and give and take. On the other hand, in 1867 the area of Canada west of the lakehead was only sparsely populated. After the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway the situation changed. In addition to those Canadians who travelled west from other parts of Canada, people from many lands came to our shores to join with the two founding races in the experience of nation building. My experience in Ottawa and in the west has shown me that the millions of Canadians who now populate our nation west of the lakehead have their own unique, dynamic and meaningful concept of Cana-dianism, as do other regions of Canada. It is possible that political, economic and social developments in Canada over the past years have accentuated regional points of view. If this is the case, then I for one feel it constitutes one of the basic strengths of Canada founded on the idea of unity in diversity. The time has come, however, to minimize the possibility of misunderstanding, and this is another reason why we should hold the series of conferences which I have suggested.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Quebec a legislative committee is well advanced in its study of our constitution. Soon it will report on its work and make recommendations. Is this not another reason why the federal government should take the initiative and set up a series of constitutional conferences? I think the answer from the fathers of confederation would be, yes.
I should like to make a few brief closing observations in the area of our party's principles. I believe that apart from the responsibility the federal government has for maintaining social and economic standards throughout the land we should insist that the

government which spends the tax dollar should be obliged to raise it.
There is another principle, sir. It is my opinion that a great disservice is done when the ordinary fiscal problems connected with federal-provincial relations are confused with the larger question of bilingualism and bi-culturalism. I fully realize that many of my province's aspirations-legitimate aspirations -relate to economic considerations; but currently too many people both inside and outside Quebec are confusing the normal demands for the tax dollar with the auestion of English-French relations. The results are harmful, sir. Men in responsible public positions should realize that the words "nation", "state" and "province"-and these are just examples-do not always have the same meaning in both the official languages of our country.
Take one translation. For example, "de-mander" in French means "to ask for", but when somebody is speaking in French in the province of Quebec and says "demander", invariably it gets translated in the English newpapers of the country as a "demand" from the province of Quebec. It is said the people of Quebec say, "We will have our way by demanding this, or else". But it does not mean "demand". I do not want to seem to be giving the house a lecture at this time, Mr. Speaker, but this is just one example. As I say, "demander" in French means "ask for"; but invariably we see in the English newspapers outside the province of Quebec that Quebec is demanding something, when they are only asking for something.
In finishing my remarks today, Mr. Speaker, I want to make some specific criticisms relating to this legislation brought forward by the government. My criticism is directed toward the field of federal-provincial relations and the attitude thereto of this government. One year ago a centralist cabinet made up of over one third ex-senior civil servants slavishly adopted the centralist point of view. I am not exaggerating when I say that apart from a budget which, for the first time in the history of Canada, had its main parts completely withdrawn, all major aspects of the federal government's domestic economic policy floundered on the rocks because they failed to consult with the provinces in areas of conjoint jurisdiction. Municipal loans, loans to university students, the extension of the Family Allowances Act-these are only examples-and the budget itself were all key areas where the government floun-
Dominion-Provincial Relations dered on the rocks with its whole economic program.
Apart from the programs floundering, Mr. Speaker, national unity was hurt. But now the pendulum has swung to the other extreme and, as I said before, many Canadians are now fearful of the government's not stopping in the middle of the pendulum, but having gone right over-at least this is how it seems to many of us-to the extreme of decentralization. What the right hon. Prime Minister has omitted to realize is that no matter what the political stripe of the government, no matter what principle or doctrine this government bases its activities on, a federal prime minister in federal-provincial relations must defend the federal cause; he must not negotiate it. The right hon. Prime Minister did great things for this country, and I was proud of him, when he negotiated so honourably for our nation at home and abroad. I say this in a bipartisan sense. But in federal-provincial relations there are times to lead and times to negotiate. However, Mr. Speaker, the present government has negotiated far too long and has forgotten to lead in the federal cause. That is one of the real reasons why federal-provincial relations are in the state they are today, and why national unity has been hurt so much.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the house for their kind permission to continue my remarks, which I will certainly bring to an end very shortly. I would simply like to close my remarks by repeating-and I know members opposite will think I have been quite partisan in the last few minutes-that which I said at the beginning, namely that I think in this year 1965, in the area of federal-provincial relations most of us should try immediately to strike a bipartisan note and get on to bipartisan ground. I sympathize with the government because with regard to federal-provincial relations it is difficult to know exactly what to do in a young country like Canada, the first country in the western world that has attempted to combine a federal system of government with a parliamentary

Dominion-Provincial Relations system. It is not easy and I recognize that; but surely this is another reason why when we come up with alternative proposals with regard to this subject hon. members opposite should not say we are just anti-Quebec. But that is what will be said of many of us.
The government got into great trouble a year ago by slavishly adopting outmoded centralist principles, and now they have gone right through the middle of the pendulum to the extent that it seems very, very possible to many Canadians that they are advocating an exaggerated system of decentralization today. Conservatives, Mr. Speaker, fight the extremes of centralization or decentralization wherever they find them. I can only plead with the government to give serious consideration to this question.
While I have made a lengthy speech today on this subject, and while I agree with the substantive part of the legislation the government has brought before the house, I think their timing has been terrible. I believe the government should get on with the basic things which must be done in federal-provincial relations before they bring this type of detailed, ad hoc, patchwork legislation before the Canadian House of Commons. The next time they bring this kind of legislation before the House of Commons, I hope the government will have taken the initiative to really improve permanent consultative machinery between Ottawa and the provinces. I hope the government will have taken the initiative to convene a meeting with the provinces to plan public spending priorities in the social and economic fields. Third, but probably most important, I hope the government will have taken the initiative to set about this series of conferences so that we shall obtain a modern constitution suited to modern times.
If this is done, sir, I can assure members opposite that they will find members on this side of the house only too willing to discuss matters of this nature in a bipartisan sense. I for one, and I am sure this applies to many members, think that if we do this kind of thing, if we get behind principles of this kind, we stand a much greater chance-I am a realistic optimist when I say this-in a spirit of co-operation, willingness and with a broad view, of really having something to celebrate about in 1967.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many who believe that there are no fundamental differences between the two major parties in this country. I see in the
[Mr. Grafftey.l
kind of legislation which has been introduced by this government over the last 18 months to two years a pattern which separates me as far from their philosophy-and farther-as I am from those on my left. There are fundamental differences, notwithstanding what members of the fourth estate may write in this connection; and what I have read indicates-as is often the case-that they, like the spectators, are often behind the play. I can do no better than put on the record at the outset the statement of those principles from which stem my beliefs in this matter of opting out and the constitutional problems confronting the country generally.
This is the view of Sir John A. Macdonald when he was speaking in the confederation debates, as reported at page 33:
Ever since the union-
He was speaking of the United States of America.
__was formed the difficulty of what is called
"state rights" has existed, and this had much to do in bringing on the present unhappy war in the United States. They commenced, in fact, at the wrong end. They declared by their constitution that each state was a sovereignty in itself, and that all the powers incident to a sovereignty belong to each state, except those powers which, by the constitution, were conferred upon the general government and congress. Here we have adopted a different system. We have strengthened the general government. We have given the general legislature all the great subjects of legislation. We have conferred on them, not only specifically and in detail all the powers which are incident to sovereignty, but we have expressly declared that all subjects of general interest not distinctly and exclusively conferred upon the local governments and local legislatures shall be conferred upon the general government and legislature.
These words were quoted by Prime Minister St. Laurent in this House of Commons on January 31, 1949, as reported at page 88 of Hansard for that year.
Rather than finding new ways to divide the nation the government should be searching, in my view, for an opting in program rather than an opting out program. There has been no indication of that, that I have been able to see. The course has been exactly the same from the beginning. This is a curious reversal from a government which over 22 years was the all-powerful government of policies on centralization.
The theory of two nations was enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) at Murray Bay on August 17, 1963. This enunciation was the first I had heard of the theory of a nation within a nation. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that that phrase will come back to haunt the Prime Minister. I believe that

you can speak culturally of a nation within a nation: But politically you cannot have a nation within a nation, and still have one Canada. Yet every action of this government shows that is precisely what they have in mind-two nations, politically as well as culturally.
Never in my belief has national unity been under attack as it has been under the Pearson administration, under the Liberal administration, under Liberal policies. The tactics, as my hon. friend from Brome-Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) has just pointed out, appropriate to the United Nations do not work on the Canadian political scene. This government and its adherents have persistently taken the attitude that Quebec is to be treated as a foreign country, to be bought with concessions and shoved off in the corner to run its own affairs. To this 1 object. To this I take violent exception. A Liberal policy of gradual isolation of Quebec will ultimately result in separation. I call it deconfederation on the instalment plan. Quebec is not a foreign country. It is as much a part of Canada as Ontario, the maritimes, the west or the north. Historically it is more important. I think of the words of Henri Bourassa-
Le Canada tout entier, c'est notre patrie.
That is the true, authentic voice of Quebec speaking. It is a voice that this government does not want to hear. This government has hitched its star to the extremists, and in doing so is progressively dismembering Canada. This legislation, the opting out bill, is just one of those steps-the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has called it this, as has Mr. Lesage-perhaps a first, halting step, along the road to eventual disintegration.
From my observation this has been the attitude of the Prime Minister from the beginning. We have two flags, two pension plans, opting out, a constitution with the vertebra removed, Ontario adopting a modified red ensign-and other provinces will be doing the same. We have one flag for the provinces, another for federal purposes. That is the situation in which they are placing this country. We are divided, rent asunder, torn, fragmented, at a time when we are approaching the one hundredth year of confederation, a confederation that has given us freedom, prosperity and peace. My observation is that it is a very sad and shocking sight, a very far cry from the days of the visionary words of Sir John A. Macdonald which I read into the record at the outset. This is not my con-
Dominion-Provincial Relations cept of how a nation should be built. It is not my concept of how to create unity.
The Liberal premier of Saskatchewan said this to the Canadian club on October 19, 1964:
At one dominion-provincial conference after another, the provinces, faced with ever-increasing costs, are making ever greater financial demands on Ottawa. And year by year the federal authorities, for the sake of national unity, have been forced to give ground.
I ask, where does it stop? When does the government cease giving away the birthright of all Canadians, the right to a national government and to a national structure? Under the Pearson government parliament is being plucked of its powers like a chicken. Every now and then the Minister of Justice makes a speech. He talks about everything except that which we want to hear. He is amazingly voluble on some things and just as amazingly reticent on others. He made a speech in Montreal on February 27 this year, one whole section of which was devoted to "The natural interdependence of Quebec and Canada", as though they were two different countries. This is the government that talks of our interdependence with the United States. While they are paving the way for union on the one side, they are opening the door to separation on the other. In the same speech the Minister of Justice, after explaining opting out as some precious pearl in the diadem of co-operative federalism, tied it in with the constitutional amendment and said that this could be only, to quote him, "a preliminary step". One shudders to think what is coming up next in the Liberal bag of tricks.
I believe Mr. Lesage understands these matters a little better-perhaps a little better than anyone in the present federal govem-men. He says that opting out has obtained for Quebec a special status. These are his words, as quoted in the Montreal Gazette for March 4 of this year. There is another view on this special status which comes from the Louis Riel committee, published in Le Devoir for March 27:
The Louis Riel committee therefore is of the opinion that the Favreau-Fulton formula-
That is a complete misnomer. Mr. Fulton's name should not be in there at all, because this formula is so far removed from the one with which he dealt as to make him a complete stranger to it. Its dealing with section 91(1) of the act makes it so. I repeat:
The Louis Riel committee therefore is of the opinion that the Favreau-Fulton formula implies a grave danger of the balkanization of Canada, outside of which would be Quebec. Our special

Dominion-Provincial Relations status would then become the isolation of being shut out, and might better be expressed as a "singular status."
That is exactly the point I am advancing. This is not opting out: It is shutting out Quebec from confederation all along the line. One cannot separate opting out from the constitution and all the rest, because it is all part of the same theme. If it were only opting out there would be no problem; but it involves the whole course of this government. Certainly the argument on the constitutional changes applies directly to opting out, because they are directly linked by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) in his speech, and by the premier of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, in his remarks in the legislature of Quebec.
Sir John A. Macdonald's view was that there should be a strong central government. This was Cartier's view and this was George Brown's view. I quoted Macdonald from page 33 of the confederation debate, speaking on February 4, 1865 where he outlined the dangers of so-called "states rights", and the manner in which that philosophy had erupted into civil war in the United States-which the fathers of confederation in Canada tried to avoid and did avoid by giving the residual powers to the federal government. They were right then, and those who stand for a central government having the capacity to discharge its responsibilities are just as right now, because anything less than that would mean the fragmentation of this country.
The Prime Minister of Canada has been almost indecent in his haste to give away what Canadians in every province and territory of this country have spent 100 years in building. He has praised the constitution with faint damns. He has characterized it as obsolete and archaic. He has said that we must reshape it, revamp it and rebuild it. In 1963 he said that we needed a 1963 model. No doubt now in 1965 he is suggesting that we need a 1965 model. He has shifted with every wind, swayed with every change in temperature, sought on all occasions to please, to concede, to surrender, to give in, as long as no one is going to get annoyed with this pristine Liberal government-this aggregation of Simon pures on the treasury benches. What a farce, Mr. Speaker, I say.
On November 26 at the federal-provincial conference the Prime Minister said this:
No constitution can provide in all of these matters, a clear and rigid separation of the functions, responsibilities and powers of our respective governments-
It did, until they over there started fooling around with it; tinkering and tampering in

a field in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is an expert.
The allocation of powers in the British North America Act is in the clearest language imaginable. There are exclusive federal powers and there are exclusive provincial powers, and in a few areas the power is shared. The residue belongs to this parliament. It should be noted that the powers are not allotted to this or that government-and opting out is indirectly in this area-but to the central parliament or the provincial legislatures.
Thus, when a weak federal government sits around a table in secret sessions with the provinces, in what is rapidly becoming the fourteenth parliament of this country, and arrives at secret decisions, it is not the federal government that is giving up its own powers, but the powers of the parliament of all the people of Canada. These are being sold down the river-and I repeat "sold down the river"-to satisfy the exigencies of the Prime Minister's view of practical politics. That is all it amounts to-the buying and selling of our national patrimony; the negotiation of the national structure. This is one thing that is not negotiable as long as parliament has even a scintilla of responsibility.
The premier of Quebec believed that in 1949 and the present Prime Minister also believed that in 1949. On February 15 of that year the Prime Minister said in parliament that to accord a veto to the provinces would place this country in a "constitutional strait-jacket" which would make "progress and development quite impossible". This is exactly what he is now attempting to do. Where is the responsibility or the logic in such an abrupt about-face? Did the Prime Minister know then what he was talking about, or does he not know now?
At the conference in 1963 he was the first to speak and he produced the opting out offer before even being asked. The Prime Minister said at that time:
One can readily conceive of a new arrangement involving transfer to the provincial governments of full responsibility for some of the present shared-cost programs. Such a transfer would be carried out on a scale that would involve hundreds of millions of dollars.
What a delightful carrot to place before the provincial premiers even before the conference got under way. This was hundreds of millions of dollars voted by this parliament in respect of specific programs in which the federal government would be playing a part, being shovelled out at federal-provincial conferences by the Prime Minister, starving

for support. All this money, in the words of the Minister of Finance used in this house a day or two ago, if I heard him correctly, would go to the provinces opting out and producing new programs-not the same ones, but different ones, in accordance with clause 12, having substantially the same objectives as those approved by this parliament.
Under that criterion I suggest to the Minister of Finance that two programs as radically different as the Soviet cosmonaut program and the Zambian space project-oil drums and all-would get the same cash remuneration. Although radically unlike both certainly have "substantially the same objective". The whole thing takes on an air of unreality, but that is customary when dealing with the projected legislation of this government. At the same federal-provincial conference, after falling all over himself to offer the provinces the most colossal handout of the people's money in Canadian history, the Prime Minister made one of his statesmanlike assertions. He said:
We are seeking by co-operation to make our federal system work to the best advantage of all Canadians.
After that revolutionary opening he went on to say:
This can be done on the basic principles established in 1867.
I have just read those basic principles from the debates which took place in 1865. Cooperative federalism from the point of view of Liberal policy as practised by this government means the dismantling of our constitutional structure and the surrender of national sovereignty. It represents the progressive fragmentation of federal authority, and it means placing this parliament in the deep freeze.
The basic principles established in 1867 were ruthlessly scrapped on October 14, 1964 and this Prime Minister, for whatever short time he may have left, will go down in history as the man who drove a wedge into the constitution of Canada and, in so doing, into confederation itself. I think it should be pointed out also that prior to the enactment of the constitution and prior to any judicial interpretations of that act in subsequent years, there were those, in particular some hon. members from Canada east, who took part in the confederation debates. I do not know if my hon. friend has seen fit to read any other passages than those of Sir John A. Macdonald or whether his party recognizes any of the other fathers of confederation. I think any student of constitutional history in this land, no matter how slight his knowledge may be, would agree with the fact that the judicial interpretation of the British North America Act has resulted in a great proportion of the residual powers being vested in the provinces rather than in the federal government. If I may straighten the record which has been distorted to some degree by the last speaker, I would say this has been a problem of Canada since these judicial interpretations left the provinces with the vast majority of economic, social and judicial powers, while the federal government was

Dominion-Provincial Relations given the vast majority of the taxing powers. Then, following the Rowell-Sirois report in 1938, this house used those taxing powers to remedy the difficult situation at the end of the depression and the subsequent period of war. These federal powers were used to a far greater degree in the national interest than the constitution of this country, as it has evolved and as it has been interpreted by the courts, actually permitted.
If there is one thing that distinguishes between the reactionary, who has his head in the past and his foot in the deep, deep past and the realist in political life, it is that the realist can distinguish between present needs, present trends and the present desires of the people of Canada, and what has occurred in the past. It has been characteristic of this administration that since it took office it has recognized this fact. The opting out bill before us, along with other measures such as the municipal loan fund, recognizes that the trend to centralization which was the natural trend of the thirties, to get out of the depression, and the inevitable trend of the war years has now been reversed, and that what is needed today is power, authority, and the wealth with which to carry out obligations for development at the provincial level.

He looks back on the halcyon days from 1957 to 1963 when this nation was apparently unified as never before; when there was no friction between the various parts of the nation; when, apparently, there was absolute harmony between the French Canadian part of our partnership and the rest of Canada.
