I think a lot of this is not altogether an accurate description of what the situation is. You need and must have a strong central government, as you must have strong provincial governments, each acting within the scope of the necessary authority which provincial governments and a federal government must have in a federal system of government. There is no question about that. I think it is a case of rendering unto Ottawa the things which belong to Ottawa and rendering unto the provinces the things which must belong to the provinces. It is this failure to conceive of this division for which later during the course of my remarks I will lay strong blame upon the government, because I think they have been derelict in their duty. I refer not only to this government but to the government of the Liberal party which persisted for some 22 years.
This is a debate, Mr. Speaker, which I hope will become not only a debate in this house but a great national debate throughout the country. This must come about if we are to solve what I think is the most difficult and persistent problem which this country will have to face for a number of years, namely the division and distribution of parliamentary powers and taxing privileges between these two forms of government. On the other hand, I think it would be a shameful thing if, in our attempt to do this, during the course of this debate any effort was made to whip up the fires of racial and regional
Dominion-Provincial Relations anger and hostility, prejudice and bigotry. I feel that this is something which must be avoided, and we in this house owe it as a duty to our country and our constituents, as well as to our party to make sure that this is not done.
The greatest difficulty-and this particular bill brings the problem to the fore-is how we are going to arrange for the distribution of powers between the two levels of government. There is no virtue per se in centralization. There is no sin per se in decentralization. Coming from the constituency I do, living in an area remote from the centres of government both provincial and federal, it has been our experience in the frontier lands of the north that too much centralization was not a good thing. We found it difficult, being remote and having no considerable measure of representation, to secure from the levels of government those legislative measures required for the development of our frontier lands. For this reason, when we talk of centralization and decentralization we must consider this particular fact.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) put his finger on a very acute difficulty in this whole issue. This country of Canada may be compared to a great bowl, with Quebec and Ontario, being in the centre, at the bottom. Everything has a natural tendency to come down to the centre. This natural tendency has been accentuated by two other steps which have been taken, one of which was mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax. For a great many years the protective tariff has permitted in the central part of the country the development of manufacturing areas and resources which, under different circumstances, might well have gone elsewhere; I do not think there is any question about that. I have heard it argued that it would have been a better thing had the fathers of confederation settled upon a unitary system of government. I disagree with that view very strongly indeed, Mr. Speaker. If in a country like Canada we did have a unitary system of government, then much as I admire my colleagues and the people in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, at this time more than one half of the people living in the areas of Canada outside of those two provinces would now be living in those provinces, and a large part of our industry would also be situated there.
In addition to the protective tariff there is another special measure which I think points in the same direction. With regard to the problems of transportation, the question of

Dominion-Provincial Relations rail freight rates was the subject of discussion during the lengthy hearings of the MacPherson royal commission. Legislation was subsequently introduced and this has now been discussed by a committee of this house. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the effects of the type of freight rate controls and horizontal increases in freight rates which have been perpetrated for many years has placed upon the shoulders of people living outside of the central provinces a very, very substantial burden. This, of course, has been explained many times. By reason of the competitive situation prevailing in Ontario in particular vis-a-vis water transportation, the railroads are compelled, in seeking increases in freight rates, to have recourse to the areas outside of the central part of Canada. It is my suggestion that in order to meet this and other situations we must have strong provincial governments, acting, however, within the sphere of what is proper provincial authority. I think that for anyone to suggest that we should weaken the provincial governments and vest that power in a central government would not be to the benefit of this country of Canada. Certainly, judging by what I have heard so far this has not been the voice of this party; and I am quite sure that if this policy is pursued the voice of us on this side of the house will have to be heard.
Let me examine for a minute some of the functions which strong provincial governments, acting within the proper sphere of their authority, have been able to bestow upon the people within these provinces. I am just going to deal with some very recent measures which have been taken. The province of British Columbia, acting within the sphere of its authority in connection with the construction of a railway into the north and the construction of development dams for the production of power, has been able, acting as a province, to aid in the development of resources in that province, and in a general way to be useful in aiding the general development of Canada.
The provinces of Manitoba and Nova Scotia, through the medium of measures of industrial development geared to the smaller communities, have very considerable achievements to their credit.
With regard to the province of Quebec, I am one of those who admire the spirit of adventure and progress which that province has been displaying in the last few years, with the hope, within the limits of proper provincial authority, of advancing and bene-


fiting the people of that province. I think it compares with the sense of achievement that we on this side of the house, through the policy of national and northern development of our government in 1958, were able to bring to the people of Canada as a whole. I respect and admire the people of Quebec for what they are doing in this regard.
I leave, Mr. Speaker, this part of my remarks by emphasizing once more that there is no case which can be made for the weakening of provincial authority. Certainly I do not think that anyone on this side of the house is attempting to make such a case. Provincial governments must be maintained strongly, but maintained strongly within the limits of what must be proper provincial jurisdiction.
I should like now to make some comments about the statement made by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene). There is no doubt, as my hon. friend for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) said, that the original conception of Sir John A. Macdonald and the fathers of confederation was to provide for the residuary powers being allotted to the central government. They attempted to achieve this by placing in the initial clause 91 the words "enacting measures for peace, order and good government". However, by means of litigation rather than legislation as a result of a number of cases taken to the privy council, this situation did not continue, with the result that something other than what was intended by the fathers of confederation was brought about. The law lords of England came to the conclusion, which could not of course be appealed and which has thus been written into our constitution, that the residuary powers should really be allotted to the provincial governments under the heading of property and civil rights.
It is as a result of this change that we find ourselves in the present difficult situation, facing problems which the mind of man could not even consider in 1867. These decisions by the privy council have resulted in the fact that we now find ourselves with provincial governments charged with responsibility in many areas in respect of which unfortunately the smaller provinces do not have the financial resources.
The hon. member for Renfrew South said that the present Liberal government has accepted the constitution as it is. I suggest that is a grave error which this government has made and I propose to deal with it in a moment.

Before leaving our consideration of the bill itself, I should like to make one or two more comments. Most of the provisions can be considered during our clause by clause study in the committee of the whole, but there is no doubt that the bill simply permits the provincial governments to continue to administer those programs involving subject matters which lie exclusively within provincial jurisdiction. It permits the provincial governments to continue to administer these programs, but with a change in the method by which financing is to be arranged. Surely that is the net result of this legislation. This may well be the result desired because of problems which have arisen between federal and provincial governments as to the interpretation of these programs.
In examining the Auditor General's report for the year ending March 31, 1962, I find he has said this:
-the audit office opinion was restated that the Unemployment Assistance Act, administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare, includes ambiguities which have resulted in varying interpretations, and that the text merits further consideration.
The Unemployment Assistance Act is one of the measures covered by this bill. The Auditor General repeated that statement in the report for the years ending March 31, 1963 and 1964. It is quite obvious for this reason that it is not a bad idea to have this kind of legislation vested in the provinces, subject of course to the necessity of requiring the provinces to establish to the satisfaction of the federal government that they are administering these programs to the same extent as they were under any previous arrangement. This is probably highly desirable, because instead of having two civil services, provincial and federal, dealing with the question, we would only have the one provincial administration. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will be subjected to very close questioning about this subject, in order that hon. members may be satisfied that the provincial governments will have to undertake to enter into agreements by which these programs will be maintained and carried out in a manner at least as good as or better than before.
One benefit I can envisage in this regard is that the provincial governments would have an unfettered use of this money and could perhaps carry on the same services at a lower cost. Or, conversely, they might be able to use the same amount of money and provide better programs. These are possibilities I can envisage under the provisions of
Dominion-Provincial Relations this bill but I think they are the only possible benefits which might accrue from it.
For the above reasons, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should ask why the legislation was passed. The hon. member for Renfrew South has suggested that the present government accepts the constitution as it is. That being the case, the government is making a grave mistake. The difficulties we find ourselves now facing, and the real issue which this country must face very shortly is, how are we going to rearrange legislative responsibility and how are we going to reallocate the division of power between the federal and provincial governments. How are we going to redistribute taxation privileges in light of changing conditions and the conditions which now prevail following almost 100 years of confederation, and in light of the decisions of the privy council to which I referred? These decisions have obviously placed burdens on the shoulders of provincial governments which originally were not intended to be borne by the provinces. There must be redivision and reallocation, and the fault of this government is that it has only played around at the edges of these difficulties rather than face up to them.
The government has established a royal commission on bilingualism and bicultural-ism, and I do not discount the efforts of that commission because it has its use; but this does not touch upon the real nub of the problem. We have had a flag debate here in this chamber. Although I cannot discuss it, I can say that it also did not go to the heart of the issue, but remained on the perimeter. We have been faced with the problem of establishing a contributory pension scheme, and we are now attempting to work out an opting out formula. We must also face the difficulties involved in establishing legislation for amending our constitution. All these things may be of some use, but I am afraid that we are neglecting the real issue in the method by which we are attempting to redivide constitutional powers.
We must be realistic and realize that there was a very ancient and deep-seated hostility in Europe between the two Canadian founding races for many hundreds of years. We must recognize that this hostility was exported to this continent and has persisted here to some extent in a political form. That political hostility has never been very far from the surface but always there ready to bubble up when encouraged by irresponsible people in public life and elsewhere.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
The good will which must exist in Canada between the two founding races can be compared to a bank account. It has never been very large or extravagant, but I am afraid that as a result of these peripheral measures -the royal commission, the flag debate, the pension bill, the opting out legislation and the amending formula with regard to the constitution-by thus exacerbating the issues we are drawing cheques against this bank account, and soon we are going to have to face the real problem of finding a means by which we can redivide the constitutional authority in this country, at which time we will find that there is nothing left in the account.
Just the other day the Prime Minister announced that the question of the increase in steel prices was going to be referred to the economic council. This is a very nice gesture but it is absolutely meaningless. No federal government has any power or authority to deal with prices. No matter what the economic council may find, the ambit of authority does not lie within the four corners of the federal constitution. Only in the case of an emergency under the peace, order and good government provision is it possible, as it was during the war, for this to be done.
A short time ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) indicated that in his opinion the combines legislation was not as effective as it might be. He intimated he was giving some consideration to broadening the base of this legislation and this jurisdiction from criminal law by drawing on the trade and commerce provisions. This matter has been the subject of judicial consideration, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think there is any doubt but that, without an expression of willingness on the part of the provincial governments to render to the federal government a measure of the authority they now hold, without an expression of willingness on the part of the provincial governments to give to the federal government some authority with regard to the question of price fixing, it is impossible for the federal government to deal with these problems which in the very near future may become problems that are national emergencies in scope.
We look ahead not too many years when, having in mind the increase in population, we will be faced with problems of water pollution and air pollution and with regard to the conservation of rivers and lakes. These are matters that lie squarely within provincial jurisdiction. They cannot long be ignored on the national level. Before too long it will be


necessary for negotiations to commence between the two levels of government for the purpose of seeking to have the provincial governments convey to the federal government some measure of authority, even if on a joint basis, to deal with these pressing problems. When that time comes we may find that conditions as between different regions of this country may have been so exacerbated by measures of this kind that we are now considering that we will fail in our desire to obtain the consensus we must have to achieve these changes. This is the complaint I have against the government and the Prime Minister, that they have been playing around the edges and have refused to come to grips with the real problem, the reallocation of powers between the two levels of federal and provincial authority.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are considering Bill No. C-142, introduced last March 13 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon).
A close examination of the bill shows that it is in a sense the implementation of the cooperative federalism formula, and especially so considering the statement of the Minister of Finance, as reported on page 12483 of Hansard:
A province, to contract out of a joint program, must enter into an agreement with the federal government. The bill empowers the governor in council to authorize the Minister of Finance and the federal minister responsible for the administration of the joint program to enter into an agreement with a province.
We are told that this Bill No. C-142 will allow provinces to opt in or opt out of shared programs. On the other hand, a closer examination of the bill will show that they have no alternative, that their only choice is that they can negotiate with the federal government concerning existing shared programs. They are not free to withdraw from existing joint programs or to change them. There is therefore no option, because there is federal control. The provinces are under the sway of the federal government and the whole structure of this bill indicates that provinces will be limited in years to come.
Under this bill or under co-operative federalism the provinces will continue to be tied to the federal government and will not be free to opt out of shared programs. They can only accept what will be decided by the Minister of Finance who will still retain the necessary authority to accept or reject the proposals of the provincial governments.

This means that in the future, the provincial governments, under the provisions of Bill No. C-142, will have to eat out of the federal government's hand, so to speak. The provinces will still be under the sway of the federal government which keeps control over all taxation powers.
The government will continue to levy taxes and it will grant the provinces only what it wishes to give them. The federal government still retains control over inspectors for the various joint programs and the appointment of officials who will still have something to say in any future negotiating of those joint programs.
In short, the federal government retains control as at present. The only privilege given to the provinces under this bill is the power to negotiate.
For a long time we have been spelling out in the house our position respecting the central government. As regards the legislative or other powers of the provinces, the federal government should cease once and for all to be the authority monopolizing all taxes and all taxation responsibilities.
The federal government took over all the taxation fields and then said to the provinces: Come and eat in my hand if you want to develop any sector of the economy. The provinces will therefore have to keep on going to Ottawa to get the few cents that should be theirs or the taxation powers granted them under confederation.
The federal government stole some taxation fields from several provinces. Today, it would like to give them a few cents, a few crumbs in return for what it has stolen from them over many years, particularly since the war.
Everywhere we see school boards, municipalities, even social bodies make constant representations to the various provincial governments in order to obtain further sources of revenue which would enable them to meet their obligations more easily.
Following the new formula or, if you prefer, the continuation of the formula set forth in Bill No. C-142, the provincial governments will in turn continue to make representations to Ottawa to obtain crumbs in order to meet the obligations they have under their jurisdiction.
The fields of taxation which the provinces held before the war should be given back to them. There should be an end to the hypocrisy of co-operative federalism, an hypocrisy established as a legislative system under which the provinces will still be compelled to beg, to
Dominion-Provincial Relations eat out of the hand of the federal government, in short to make representations every year to obtain a few crumbs in order to meet responsibilities which, from both the legislative and legal points of view, are theirs.
We are told that the measure before us will result in a transfer of $900 million to the provinces. A transfer, yes, but on the terms of the federal government, according to the mood of the Minister of Finance in the future.
We are told of a transfer of $900 million, but last year, according to the figures given to us, the province of Quebec alone lost $278 million, an amount which is subscribed to the federal government as direct and indirect, hidden or official taxes. That amount of $278 million has not been given back to the province.
The sources of taxation of the provincial governments should be given back to them; those governments should no longer be compelled to come to Ottawa; in short, the government should stop telling us, under the pretence of co-operative federalism, that agreements have been reached with the provincial governments, while the situation should be what it was before the war, that is to say, the provinces should still have their sources of taxation, which would be the logical way to allow them to meet their obligations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill No. C-142 is one of the last basic pieces of legislation that will be brought before us during this session, but it is extremely important because, once again it concerns the problem of Canadian unity and the future of confederation, since it deals with relations between the central government and the provinces.
This matter raises special interest at the present time in view of the resurgence now taking place in all areas within the French Canadian community. French Canadians today are facing a dilemma which is indeed the problem of Canada as a whole. French Canadians wonder whether they can develop and preserve their entity in a system where, owing to the force of circumstances, they are condemned to remain in a state of perpetual minority.
English Canadians are wondering whether the aspirations of French Canada are really consistent with their views of a united and dynamic Canada: One Canada, one nation.
Canada constitutes one country only, one political entity. In a sense, we live in a united

country, out within that political Canada there are two nations, certainly two peoples with a different history, different origins, cultures and traditions, and using two different languages.
An affirmative answer can be given to both previous questions, on one condition: The French Canadian must be able to find among his English speaking fellow citizens, that is among the majority, friends or allies who, ih the first place, believe in the survival of his group; second, judge it desirable; and third, accept to set up a policy that will allow for that fact. It is therefore necessary for my English speaking colleagues to recognize certain facts that are basic for their French Canadian fellow citizens, and here are some of them:
First, of all it must not be forgotten that confederation is the result of the pact between two peoples. Historically speaking, we only have to refer to the conferences held before the birth of confederation to realize that at that time, the fathers of confederation who represented both groups then living in Canada, had set their minds on the signing of a pact or agreement. Had it been otherwise, one can wonder whether French Canada would have accepted the confederate pact of 1867.
The British North America Act, Canada's constitution, is undoubtedly a pact. I will spare you a recital of the various rulings to that effect made by the highest courts of the land and by the privy council in London to which Canada need no longer appeal since 1948.
In addition, some secondary characteristics of the confederative pact lead us to believe that it is an agreement, a contract entered into by four provinces, namely Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. It later became law through an imperial act enacted by the parliament of London which approved this constitution as a pact.
Each of those peoples in Canada is entitled to full development. Consequently, we should have the necessary ways and means to reach this objective.
We must admit that the minority group is entitled to some safeguards which, besides those granted in the constitution, protect its language and officially recognize its status and national entity.
This situation exists in every country where there are two or more cultures, but even more so in a country like ours where the culture of the majority group is also that of a great neighbouring nation, the most powerful in the world.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
The English citizens of this country must recognize that the province of Quebec is not a province like the others. Anyway, are there two absolutely identical provinces in this country?
Is there a geographical similitude between the provinces of British Columbia and Newfoundland, or between Saskatchewan and New Brunswick? Every province has its peculiar environment. And the province of Quebec, because of its history, its culture and its mission, is not a province like the others, since its role consists in safeguarding the French culture and the French language outside its geographical territory.
This difference of interpretation, which allows two groups to face but not understand each other, is probably due to the fact, as was brilliantly pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), that words do not have the same meaning in English and in French.
Indeed, for my English speaking colleagues and for the English Canadian population of this country, the word "nation" means "state"; hence, the argument that there should be a single "state-nation" in Canada. This is the point the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) tried to develop in his speech, to which I listened with great interest and which I intend to review a little later on.
For the French Canadian, the word "nation" expresses the concept of a people, of a civilized community having its own institutions it wants to keep. It is in that sense that the province of Quebec is different from the others; but the people of that province aspire to the same ideal of Canadian unity, by working to form a Canadian people and a Canadian history.
We, French Canadians, wish to co-operate in building up a strong and prosperous country. We do not want privileges. We do not want special rights. We only want one thing: that the Canadian constitution be fully respected.
That is why I do not propose to speak now about Quebec balkanization; I will deal with that later on.
I was saying that the citizens of the province of Quebec do not want privileges. They are only asking that the Canadian constitution be fully respected. That is why the great majority of the people of the province of Quebec are supporting Bill No. C-142 brought forward by the government.
I should like to refer to a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon)

Dominion-Provincial Relations when he introduced this bill, as reported on page 12482 of Hansard for March 17:
For example, a good many of these programs, and certainly the largest of them, fall primarily within provincial jurisdiction, and perhaps that should be emphasized.
The purpose of this bill is to enable the provinces to take full advantage of the Canadian constitution. One may wonder whether the ten provincial premiers have not analysed this question, since, whatever may be their political affiliation, they have all seen in this measure a piece of legislation that could be used to return to the provinces those taxation powers which, unfortunately, had been taken away from them or which they had yielded to the central government during the war in 1941. Because of the national emergency, the Liberal government of the day had called upon the provinces to yield their taxation fields, and the provinces agreed without reservation.
But where the Liberal government of the day misled the provinces was when it lured them with the idea that this concession was only temporary, that is for the duration of the war. And we recall the struggle put up by those two great premiers who have left their mark in Canada's history, Premier Duplessis of Quebec and Premier Hepburn of Ontario who, in 1948, at one of the very first federal-provincial conferences, proclaimed the need for provincial autonomy. And it was then that the people of the provinces realized that there was a condemnable encroachment on the part of the federal government, which had undertaken to withdraw from certain fields of taxation the moment war ended, when after three years had gone by, the Liberal government, the centralizer of that time, was still maintaining the economic hold that prevented the provinces from implementing and developing their policies and programs.
Now, a disguised formula, the equalization payments, was devised to satisfy the provinces which were different from Quebec. Since this economic system could not be as disastrous for them as for the province of Quebec, they accepted that arrangement which gave them back certain taxation fields coming under their own jurisdiction.
It will be recalled that the Conservative party introduced for the first time, in 1960, an option formula to solve the problem of university grants. At the time the Barrette-Sauve-Fleming formula was greeted with great enthusiasm.
If that formula was excellent in 1960-61, why would it be unworkable in other fields
[Mr Paul.]

today? Throughout its history the Conservative party has always been, in its philosophy and its policies, the defender of provincial rights and autonomy.
One may wonder whether this party, today, keeps going in the same direction.
For my part, I could not understand the difference of opinions which arose between the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), whom I congratulate for his excellent speech on the subject and who showed the practical meaning of provincial autonomy, and his colleague for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who contradicted him this afternoon by talking about a balkanization, a fragmentation of the provinces.
I will come back to that, Mr. Speaker, but right now I would like to talk about the objectivity of the bill under consideration. The Liberal party introduces this measure under the guise of co-operative federalism. It does not deserve much credit for giving back to the provinces what it took away from them. It should not try to be taken for the great supporter of provincial autonomy because, to all practical purposes, this bill does not give anything more to the provinces. It simply recognizes the economic principle it has followed and considers to be false, namely that a government can collect money or taxes and that this money can be spent by another government.
The Liberal party is to blame for making such publicity before introducing this bill because it is basically faulty in that it transfers taxation rights to the provinces conditionally only. It is not a total and absolute recognition of the rights of the provinces in certain fields of taxation.
What can be said against the bill introduced by the Minister of Finance? It has been designed only for a period of transition, since he mentioned that the period extending from the passing of the bill until 1970 or 1971 for certain programs would be experimental, while it would enable the provinces to introduce a certain legislation, so as to give back to them some fields of taxation coming under their jurisdiction.
He shows good will, but is he really determined to go on? I have no doubt that he will be eager to correct this anomaly in the bill which gives the federal government a right to control this legislation. In fact, he acknowledges himself that the federal government has legislated in certain fields of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, as I said a moment ago, in his speech of March 17. If the provinces are given back certain powers
12S67

of taxation, why should the federal government keep any control and impose its will with regard to the administration of money granted to the provinces taking advantage of this legislation?
Mr. Speaker, this is a step forward taken by the federal government, the Liberal party. I am glad to note a certain conversion in that party because, if, in the past, it has been the party of centralization, we must now give it credit for having recognized that the provinces have the right to legislate in fields related to the shared programs listed in the appendix of Bill No. C-142.
The provinces have accepted the principle of this bill introduced by the minister. This brings me to disagree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), even though he put forward learned and sound arguments in reply to the remarks of the Minister of Finance. I do not question his good faith when he introduced his amendment. Let me read it over with you. It is to be found on page 12489 of Hansard for March 17, 1965, and I quote:
That Bill C-142 be not read a second time until further consideration has been given to the priorities of their requirements desired by the provinces of Canada and its territories in those fields of jurisdiction indicated in the schedules of the said bill, such priorities to be established at a federal-provincial conference convened for the said purpose.
Is not this measure dilatory and unacceptable? If the legislation is good, why delay its passage? Why not simply ask the committee on taxation to speed up the analysis of the situation in order to establish priorities in respect to the various programs likely to be inserted in this legislation and afterwards analysed? I shall therefore take the liberty to disagree with my hon. friend from Edmonton West and to vote against his amendment.
I disagree with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) even more, when he refers to the balkanization of Quebec. What does he mean by balkanization? I wish he had given us some definition. When he speaks about Bill C-142 as a surrender of the federal government to the provinces, he is mistaken, for he should know that some legislative powers are granted to the provinces by the constitution. He is shocked because the federal government might hand over $900 million. There is nothing shocking in a repentant government handing over to the provinces the money illegally taken from them since 1941. There is nothing shocking, because it is in accordance with and provided in the con-
Dominion-Provincial Relations stitution. The federal government has legislated in fields coming under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. If the federal government is handing over $900 million to the provinces, we should be happy about it, because it is in accordance with the spirit and the letter of the 1867 constitution.
What does the balkanization of Quebec have to do with this? If the province of Quebec wants to take advantage of this legislation, it is because it provides us, citizens of Quebec, with a means of safeguarding the rights granted to us in the constitution.
It is of little importance to us that this bill be introduced by a Liberal or a Conservative government. What really matters to us, who want to contribute to the progress and the greatness of our country and who wish to be respected in accordance with the 1867 pact, is the fact that we find in it a means for the provinces to have some of their fiscal rights acknowledged.
The operation of these plans by the province of Quebec must not lead to the conclusion that our fellow citizens entertain the idea of dissociating themselves from the rest of Canada. Absolutely not. Unfortunately, there are too many people for whom Quebec's aspirations mean separatism. No, Mr. Speaker, we are not separatists, we simply want to do our share so that all the rights of all Canadian citizens will be respected and not curtailed in any way. In return, we want to get what is guaranteed to us under the constitution.
We do not want any privileges, but we believe that through the full respect of the spirit of the Canadian constitution, we shall find the necessary safeguard to prevent us from joining with all those agitators whom we could call separatists or half-separatists.
As I said earlier, the Conservative party was once the party of provincial autonomy, but within its ranks there seems to be an adverse tendency now. I would surely be vexed with myself for not congratulating the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) who spoke this afternoon about the Canadian constitution problem in such a masterly way. He did not talk about the "balkanization of Canada or of Quebec". On the contrary, and thanks to his legal knowledge, he was able to suggest a way of reconsidering perhaps the Canadian constitution, so that the two main nations composing it may keep on respecting one another and, in agreement with the other minorities in this country, work toward the development of Canada as a whole.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Mr. Speaker, it is only through the action of a sincere and earnest team that the experienced, informed and forward-looking Canadians who have freed themselves from old bonds will be able to build the future Canada, strong, vigorous, free, a reflection on the American soil of two great cultures, developing freely and contributing, each in its own way, to the enrichment of the whole of Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join very briefly in this discussion of Bill No. C-142, and in doing so I speak as a person who is removed from the federal-provincial squabbles, controversies and negotiations which have been going on for some months. I have no particular provincial axe to grind. There is no power play taking place in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon which would force the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) down an unpleasant road. For that reason I believe I have a perspective that would perhaps be a luxury to members of parliament who live in other provinces of Canada. This is a luxury they either cannot afford or are unwilling to assume.
I am unhappy with Bill C-142 and I will briefly map out my reasons. My unhappiness is not entirely related to the provisions of the bill itself, but rather mainly because of the principles it contains. We have here in fact this country, which has been built from sea to sea to sea, and all that remains now is for the federal government at the negotiating table to peacefully divide the spoils.
The vehicle they have chosen for this division of the loot is a negotiating table at a federal-provincial conference. The difficulty I see, which is the reason I reject this kind of action, is that if you are going to fight over a pie that is not quite big enough, the strongest and healthiest will win every time.
We in Canada in the past 20 months have been in the position of pitting a weak and vacillating Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) against determined, forceful, provincial premiers, all of whom have a mandate, which is something the present Prime Minister does not have and will never achieve. The sad fact of the matter is that the federal government has come out second best in every single federal-provincial conference that has been held.
There is one other reason I am distressed by this proposition. The governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories were not


allowed to attend these secret sessions at which deals were made. Before the minister or anyone else on that side interrupts me, I should state that I know there is no legal requirement on the government to invite the governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories to participate. However, let me remind them that there is a moral obligation on the government-an obligation that has not been recognized since this government took office-to allow those Canadians who happen to live north of the 60th parallel in this country an opportunity to sit in at the banquet table, to perhaps catch the crumbs from the pie which is being divided. The people of Canada in the northlands have as much of a stake in this kind of deal as have any other Canadian citizens. It is only because of an oversight on the part of a government which says it has built the country and it now should parcel it up that northern Canadians were not consulted in this regard.
There is another reason I am unhappy with this division. I am particularly unhappy because of the majority sponsorship. The dealings have been negotiated by the Minister of Finance. One need only remember that this man was the genius behind the Gordon commission report on Canada's economic prospects. This is the man, you will remember, who was charged with the responsibility of deciding what are Canada's economic prospects. All hon. members will remember what he said. He said, in effect, if there is no economic base in the maritime provinces, and the people out there are poor, they should move to Toronto. After all, he made a million dollars, so they can as well. That is an indication of the character of the man who is now sponsoring this legislation. This is a man who can only be described as some kind of a "Malcolm X" of the Canadian financial movement who is protecting this country in the interests of Canada from the evil to the south of us. He is the man who was going to protect us from this influence. He is the "Malcolm X" who was recently assassinated by his own brother-in-law, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), when he allowed American cars to come across the line free of duty.
There is another reason I am unhappy with this legislation. Speaking as a northerner I do not like the provisions of this bill, although not specifically because they have any relationship to the province of Quebec. I do not like them as they apply to any other province in Canada. I do not understand why it should be necessary to have different programs in provinces which decide to run their own

programs in fields such as old age assistance, blind persons allowances, disabled persons allowances, roads to resources and vocational training. It is my opinion that in order to develop this country these programs must be based on guarantees of fundamental developments in social securities of a national scope. There is no other choice for Canada.
This question I pose directly to the minister. Why should those of us who live in that 50 per cent of Canada which is not even in confederation-the Yukon and Northwest Territories-let you people crucify confederation and then get together to divide the garments? Why should we let you destroy confederation before we even get in? Why do you people not understand that the whole country, including the 50 per cent which is in Canada's northern regions, belongs to Canadians? It is Canadian land and can be developed by Canadians. This area belongs also to the people of southern Canada, particularly if you will but for a few years restrain your impatience and keep unto the federal authority that kind of strong central government required for the continued development of this country. I can guarantee the minister and all those of you who are anxious to receive money now and pull out, that if you will invest your money in the northland of Canada willingly and with a spirit you will receive in return every nickel you invest, and then some.
I have another question for the minister. Why should I as a Canadian be inhibited in travelling to or settling in any part of this country, be it Quebec, Ontario or anywhere else? Why should I not have available to me, to my family and to my aged parents the same social security measures, the same programs that are available to me where I now live? Why should I have to reapply for these benefits? Who is it over there on the treasury benches in the millionaire cabinet who believes that if you cut a horse in two it will run twice as fast?
Before the minister and his colleagues rush ahead with this legislation, or even in retrospect, I invite them to take a look around the country. Fly from here to Toronto, a favourite trip of the Minister of Finance, and take a look below you on a clear day. This country is empty. It has not been built up yet. It will never be built up if we have a government that decides it is going to divide the spoils here and now, that for our 100th birthday party we will just sit on the little bit of resources we have, on the little bit of money we have and parcel it out. There is
Dominion-Provincial Relations an old saying in the Canadian northland that goes like this: "Don't sit on your frozen assets". I direct this advice to the minister.
I invite him to fly from here to Halifax if he wants to see a country that is empty. I invite him to fly from here to Edmonton or Vancouver or, if he can muster that peculiar courage that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) occasionally does, fly into Canada's northland and take a look around. This country is empty. It is not built up. The job of confederation is more than 100 years away from completion, and I for one am not prepared as a northerner and particularly as a Canadian to have the group of ministers over on the treasury benches say that wherever the most electoral pressure comes from that is where they will spend the most money. If you do that you will perhaps have demonstrated your ability to survive in office beyond the next election, although I would not bet on that. You will have demonstrated an ability to survive politically in the short run, but you will have destroyed the hope of this country to develop into a great land.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) deserves the careful consideration of the house because it would have the effect of giving the government time to reconsider what it is doing. It would have the effect of giving the provinces and the federal government the time to meet in open session where people from all parts of the country, including the little old Northwest Territories and the Yukon, could sit in on the negotiations and get at the governments. It would give us time to take a look at the British North America Act, its division of responsibilities and its division of revenue sources, to see how well it has served us and where we are going.
The point has been made consistently in the house by other members that no change in the approach to the constitution is envisaged in Bill No. C-142 and that really all the federal government is doing is to give back to the provinces those things that they have by right. I sit in this chamber, Mr. Speaker, and I hear various causes being advanced. One which I support fully is the right to have a bilingual House of Commons and, indeed, the right of French Canadians, of whom I am one, to be able to use their own language and to have the bilingual nature of this country adequately and willingly reflected in the things we do. Inevitably the argument put forward is that there was

Dominion-Provincial Relations an agreement to this effect entered into willingly by the founding races of this country. There are other agreements that were entered into, including the agreements entered into by the province of Quebec with the federal government, and these are the agreements that the bill proposes to change. If a deal is a deal, which is the way we operate in the part of the country from which I come, what right has the province of Quebec or any other province to say that they want out of the deal now because it does not suit them? It suited the provinces very well, at the time they signed these agreements, to have the benefit of national programs and the benefit of a central government that would collect the moneys and share in these programs.
Most of the agreements covered in the bill do not expire for another two years at least. By what right can any member of this house demand that the federal government turn over to the provinces two years in advance money that they had agreed would be used to finance joint federal-provincial programs until 1967 at the earliest? This is another reason why there is ample time for the federal government to recall the provincial premiers. We will support the Prime Minister if he wants to get tough with them. He does not have to tremble every time one of the provincial premiers yelps at him. We will give him the backbone that he has apparently lacked up till now. We have agreements that are still good for at least two years if we want to insist on enforcing them, so why can the Prime Minister not take the time to renegotiate the whole business? Let him sit down with the premiers and say that we know that the demands on the provinces are increasing and that it is time a review was made of the sources of revenue. Indeed, the whole area of their responsibilities could bear some scrutiny in the light of 100 years experience, in the light of a much changed Canada.
We are not opposed to this kind of thing but we are opposed to people of mean spirit, mean ambition and, yes, mean vision. We are opposed to people of this kind deciding that in the interest of votes or in the interest of their own immediate ambition they will carve up the pie that is called Canada and pass it out to the 10 hungry provinces at a time when 50 per cent of the country is begging to be given consideration. We want to enter confederation. We want you to invest your money in our country. We want you to help us to develop our political, social and educational institutions. We want you to do these things
[Mr. Rheaume.l
and we are prepared to pay you back with interest. We do not want people like the Minister of Finance, or the premier of Quebec for that matter, carving up Canada to suit themselves. In that regard I recall the statement of the premier of Quebec in Dawson city in the election campaign of 1953. That was before he became minister of northern affairs, because that post had not yet been created for him. He was then the minister in charge of the old resources and development department.
When asked about living and working conditions for the people in the Canadian north around Dawson city in August 1953, he said: If you don't like living in Dawson city why don't you move south? Then, we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who said: If you cannot make a living in the maritimes, move to Toronto. These are the men of great spirit, great imagination with tremendously broad horizons, who are going to develop this country. All I say, Mr. Speaker, is, thank God they were not around in 1865 because if they had been this country would still consist of a little cluster of people huddling along the St. Lawrence valley. If it had been left up to them to develop the country that certainly would have been what would have happened.
I have in my reading, Mr. Speaker, come across an interesting passage in the confederation debate which can be found on page 681 of the debates on confederation. This is for February, 1865 and the hon. member who at that time represented the constituency of Oxford North was speaking on the matter then before the house. He makes the point, first of all, that it is absolutely essential for the building of Canada, for the advancement of the confederation that is being proposed, that there be a strong central authority, and that various local and regional interests will have to be sacrificed to the building of a great nation. Having made that point, which is precisely the point I am making tonight, he goes on in these words-and it is strange indeed I believe that 100 years later a member of parliament can stand up in this house and echo those words exactly. Even though we have come a long way perhaps, the problem facing us as a young nation has remained approximately the same. He says this:
Geographically this country covers a vast extent of territory. We can lean our backs on the snows of the north, and from that quarter no enemy can attack us: and if we have no great breadth from north to south, we have a large expanse westwards. Although, too, we are in a

northern clime, although our latitude is higher than that of our southern neighbour, yet this is no obstacle to the growth of population or to the increase of prosperity. Teeming millions will in future inhabit this land, and we are called upon now to lay deep and broad the foundations of a great empire. Let us shew that we value the free institutions of Britain transplanted to this soil; institutions founded upon principles of freedom and universal toleration; institutions that have made the parent land great, and that mark it out as the one bright spot in the old world to which the eyes of the nations turn when their liberties are imperilled, and as the city of refuge to which crowned heads, as well as the victims of their misrule, can alike flee for safety in the hour of their misfortune. I have no hesitation, Mr. Speaker, in endorsing the scheme before us.
In that, he and I differ because I do not endorse the bill before us. I quote again:
I accept it, further, because of the prospect it holds out to us of building up a great nationality here, and of handing down to our children institutions which our fathers have bought with their blood.
These words, Mr. Speaker, are words I direct to the Minister of Finance and to all other members of parliament, regardless of which side of this chamber they sit, and to all provincial premiers in their anxiety to divide up the pie: Be careful, all of you, if you decide that those of you who cower along the United States border are going to divide the southern 50 per cent of this country and parcel it amongst yourselves to get rich quick; you be careful, because there is a kind of separatist movement that would not take much prompting in that 50 per cent of this country that lies north of the 60th parallel.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just resumed his seat told us that Canadian unity could be safeguarded inasmuch as our French Canadian ethnic group accepts almost any sacrifice, while nobody else would accept the same sacrifices.
The hon. member stated that if we had stuck to the situation prevailing 100 or 200 years ago, our citizens would be living only on the shores of the St. Lawrence, that is if we had followed the policy of Quebec.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) is not very aware of the present situation in Canada. Moreover, he does not want to understand the interest of the province of Quebec in safeguarding national unity, without however prejudicing anybody, neither English speaking nor French speaking people. Yes, we want to save Canada, but in the most complete mutual respect of the various ele-
Dominion-Provincial Relations ments which at the present time form our Canadian nationality.
Mr. Speaker, we are considering Bill No. C-142 under which the provinces will be free to participate or not in joint programs.
I heard a while ago the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) tell us that all we have to do is respect the Canadian constitution as it was set up in 1867.
I sincerely believe that the constitution of 1867 no longer meeets the present requirements of Canada. As Her Majesty the Queen said recently in Quebec city, there is nothing surprising in the fact that we want to change, amend and improve a constitution dating back 100 years. In our opinion, the constitution of 1867 must be adapted to the present needs, that is to this day and age.
It is not enough to say, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) did, that Quebec wants to balkanize itself, or that Ottawa wants to balkanize Quebec in order to turn it into something else than a province in confederation.
We wish to be part of confederation, but on our terms, not those of Tom, Dick or Harry. We wish to be part of confederation on our own terms, those of the inhabitants of Quebec, of the people who built our province and were the cornerstone of the whole country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear Liberal members say that I am right. I am right indeed. We do not want to diminish anyone. Neither do we want to discriminate against anyone. However, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) stated, we wish to be ourselves within confederation, without discriminating against anyone.
It is really something to hear people speak of national unity and what have you, especially to hear people who do not understand anything about the province of Quebec refer to the balkanization of Quebec.
The existence of Quebec dates back to 1608, even to 1534, which means that we have been anchored to and rooted in Canada for about 400 years. Never have we demanded from anybody privileges that would not be granted to others in Canada. Never have we demanded prerogatives or rights that would not be given to other groups in Canada. This country's history is there to prove it.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
We in Quebec defended Canada against the American invasion more than 150 years ago. We have insisted on being and remaining true Canadians, without discriminating against anybody.
Today we hear some hon. members-not only English speaking members, but French speaking ones as well-say that Quebec is inclined to secede from confederation. That is not true.
We are not asking only for joint programs between the federal government and the province of Quebec. Indeed not. There are also joint programs between the other provinces and the federal government. When there is some talk about separatists and separatism, one thinks right away that the province of Quebec is involved.
Barely three weeks ago I went to western Canada on the far side of the Rockies, and did you know that I met there people as separatist as any to be found in the province of Quebec? Do you know that in Alberta, in British Columbia and in Manitoba, there are people as separatist as any to be found in Quebec? Why? It is not because they are against the province of Quebec. No. It is not because Quebec is against the rest of Canada. Not at all. It is because Ottawa infringes upon the rights and prerogatives of the provinces; that explains the wave of separatism which is sweeping Canada at the present time.
If we are to balkanize Quebec, let us balkanize the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, let us balkanize also the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, because it is illogical to talk as he did earlier, always attacking the province of Quebec.
It would seem that Quebec is the pet aversion of Canada; that it is a province that should not belong to this confederation or union of provinces.
According to the constitution we have provincial rights.
Are we accused of being socialists because we have provincial rights and prerogatives? Certainly not. In the field of education, every province is free to legislate according to its needs, its mentality, its thinking, and its will. The educational system in Manitoba, in Ontario, in Quebec, in Alberta, or in British Columbia is not quite the same. Every province is free to legislate in the field of education.
Direct taxation such as the income tax, is a field which belongs rightfully to the provinces and not to the central government in Ottawa. Today, when we see the government in Ottawa taxing us and interfering
[Mr. Caouette.l
in the field of the personal income tax, we know that those rights were handed over to Ottawa at the time of the second world war. As soon as the war was over the government in Ottawa was supposed to give back to the provinces those taxation rights. Never has the Ottawa government kept its word at that time, as it never kept it with regard to any province of Canada in this respect.
The highway system is another field of provincial jurisdiction. Will you accuse the province of Quebec of being separatist because it builds express highways from Montreal to Sherbrooke, Montreal to Quebec city or Montreal to the Laurentians?
Will you accuse Quebec of being separatist? Would you accuse British Columbia of being separatist because she is now building the most beautiful highway system ever conceived and built in the whole world? What we are seeing now in British Columbia is her business, and this is under provincial jurisdiction according to the constitution of 1967.
In the field of agriculture, we often ask the federal government how many loans have been granted to the province of Quebec and what is being done to help Quebec's agriculture. Each time without fail, we are told that Quebec has her own farm credit corporation. Ottawa has one, but it lends its money elsewhere, because the other provinces do not have such a plan. Nevertheless, the province of Quebec pays taxes at the same rate as the other Canadian provinces to serve agriculture. The federal government says that Quebec has her own farm loan board, but we still pay taxes to Ottawa even though we do not benefit from the federal farm loan program.
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) stated a moment ago, we do not ask for special privileges, and those who claim the contrary are quite mistaken. All we ask is that our rights be respected as we respect the rights of others. We ask absolutely nothing from others. We want to run Quebec as we see fit and not according to the views of others. We want to run Quebec and develop it according to its possibilities, its potential and its capacities. That is what we ask and nothing else.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, with regard to Bill No. C-142 concerning shared programs, which gives the provinces the alternative to participate or not, we believe that the federal government would be well advised to grant each of the provinces, and especially the province of Quebec, the following rights.

First, the control of its credit.
If a province has brains, manpower, intelligence, purpose, it should have the power to render possible financially what is possible materially.
When we see the shared programs, and even apart from these; when we notice in our province, for instance, in the field of hospitalization, people who apply to be admitted to a hospital and who must wait six, seven or eight months before being admitted; when we see students ready to complete their studies in medicine, for instance, at Laval University in Quebec city, who cannot be admitted because there is no room and that hundreds of young people from 18 to 20 years old are refused, then, no one, not one federal or provincial member of parliament wonders whether there is a lack of materials, engineers, physical possibilities, intelligence and manpower for the construction of universities and hospitals. The problem remains always the same; there is no money to build universities and hospitals.
Mr. Speaker, if the provinces had the control of their credit, these inadequacies would disappear.
We have been taking part for six, seven or eight months in debates concerning the establishment of new chartered banks in Canada, while the other place refuses to recognize the request, in proper form, of the government of British Columbia. Some individuals enjoy the very power which is being refused to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not dwell on this matter for I will have an opportunity to do so in a few weeks. But if two, three or ten individuals in Canada are entitled to own a Canadian chartered bank, to control or try to distribute the economic blood of the nation, then a responsible province, a responsible government, should be more than entitled to enjoy similar prerogatives and similar rights. That is why we are asking that the province of Quebec, and indeed all the other provinces, have control over credit.
Second, we are asking control over our immigration. We want to know, for instance, when Mr. Hal Banks leaves Canada or the province of Quebec and when he will return. The same thing goes for the other provinces. I could say the same thing about Lucien Rivard. We do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to prevent citizens from Poland or anywhere else from settling in Canada. But we want to know who is coming to settle at home in the province of Quebec, and who is leaving, so
Dominion-Provincial Relations that we may know exactly where we stand regarding our population. In the province of Quebec, the French Canadian majority has never prevented any minority group from claiming their rights or from being considered as equals to others.
Mr. Speaker, as I often say, an active minority group, wherever it may be, in British Columbia, Ontario or Manitoba, will always manage to make itself respected.
I give as an example to all Canada the province of Quebec. In Quebec, where we make up 85 per cent of the population and where English speaking Canadians number only 12 to 15 per cent, we can state with pride and satisfaction that this minority is treated exactly like the French speaking majority. We are happy to mention it and affirm it.
Why should not the same situation prevail in Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan? The English minority in Quebec insisted on its rights and was respected. There are French minorities in western Canada where it is asked that a C.B.C. radio and television station be put in service-the Minister of Transport is in his seat and I remind him that we ask that the C.B.C. radio station in Victoria and Vancouver be made to serve that minority.
I heard a member of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), state that there was no need for French in British Columbia, because there were only very few French Canadians. When I was there two or three weeks ago, I met a group of French Canadians in Vancouver, in Victoria and in Maillardville. We are asking that the rights of French Canadians be respected there, and this hon. member replies that there is no minority problem.
Mr. Speaker, what about joint programs set up in this manner?
Fifteen per cent of the population of my area are English speaking, and I call the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) to witness, because he represents the neighbouring riding. Mr. Speaker, we will be denied these same privileges in Victoria, Vancouver, Edmonton,

Very well, Mr. Speaker. We shall deal with the sections of this bill when the house is in committee of the whole. Until then, we shall merely talk about this measure in general terms to show clearly that the province of Quebec is not so keen on joint programs.
I understand that the federal government tells us that a province may participate in a joint program or opt out of it. I believe that our province should not accept a single joint program as that would allow Ottawa to collect the taxes and later on to decide which portion will be handed back, according to the equalization formula.
In my opinion it would be more logical and more normal for Quebec to decide on its own what should be given back to Ottawa. The federal government has no business telling Quebec what to pay to Ottawa, no more than it is Ottawa's business to tell the provinces of Ontario or Manitoba what they should pay to the federal government. But it is up to the provinces to determine what can be done in order to help Ottawa maintain cohesion, understanding and some kind of unity between our Canadian provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly object to this idea. I know that we are free to participate or not to participate. However, there are always standards and legal points which compel the province to contribute to joint programs, and subsequently Ottawa decides on the amount of equalization which will be handed over to the province. Then, it is total centralization, or a complete abandonment of provincial jurisdiction.
In my opinion, Ottawa never created a province, but the provinces created the federal government. As long as we respect the full autonomy of every province, we will have a representative government, a federal government which will respect the rights of each province. This does not imply respect for the

province of Quebec only, to the prejudice of other provinces, as was said earlier by the hon. members for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) and Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who are afraid of balkanization.
We will balkanize the hon. member for Yukon when we have a system-
