Mr. Speaker, we will respect the rights of others, but we want our own rights to be respected and we do not fall into this trap of joint programs operating to the prejudice of provinces and only to the benefit of a top-heavy-I said "top-heavy"-officialdom which burdens the Canadian people with taxes.
When the federal government will have been put in step with realities and possibilities existing in Canada, provinces will be free, they will be able to develop according to their wishes, their aspirations, their possibilities, and then we will live in a happy Canada, in a land of satisfied provinces.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most important piece of legislation. Regrettably in the minds of some it seems to be something which should be tucked in at the last minute, not only the last minute of this particular sitting but the last minute of this elongated session. In this particular phase of our nation's history we have in recent months been faced with problems far greater than those which usually accost the politicians or the public. The questions we now face are not simply questions of who shall govern us, or how we shall be governed, (and a multitude of expressions could follow on that imputation), but questions concerning what kind of country we are to have. In other words, the very structure of our political organisms is constantly before us for review and consideration.
This is one of the measures, although perhaps not the most important, which deal with this over-all question of the structure of our political society. Therefore because of its tremendous importance it should not be treated as a mere afterthought.
I must start out by saying, as many of my colleagues have said, that there is, as I see it, no impropriety at all in so far as the provinces are concerned. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said that no
Dominion-Provincial Relations province is asking, through this legislation, for any special provisions. I agree with that observation, but I find that I cannot agree with most of his observations which followed.
This is not an excessive demand, nor an improper one by any province. It is not an invasion upon dominion jurisdiction. As one of the strongest and unrepentant supporters of the rights of the dominion I make this statement. I, like the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) am something less than deliriously happy with the legislation as a whole. I am impressed by the casual air about the whole thing.
We seem again to have insufficient information and possibly insufficient discussion about this legislation. I must say "possibly" because naturally being merely a Canadian citizen and a member of the senior legislative body in this country I do not know what went on at this one dominion-provincial conference at which this matter was discussed. This is one of the very important aspects of our present political situation. We are developing what practically amounts to a third area of governmental action and decision. We are almost developing a multi-governmental area of action and decision, and it is not clearcut as to where the responsibility lies. There is no channelling of information so that the responsibility may be appraised. There has been secrecy and uncertainty, and one is never sure exactly what did take place.
I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) some time ago to table the correspondence in respect of this important matter. He wrote to the premiers of the provinces on August 15, 1964, and that is a long time ago. From how many premiers were answers received? Premier Stanfield advised that the matter would be studied, and that is the last word we know of from the premier of Nova Scotia. I should like to know what the premier of Nova Scotia thinks about these things. After all, he is a representative of the oldest legislative body in this country and one of its most able and wise men. I should like to know what he thinks.
I should like to know what Premier Robarts thinks about this proposal. He is a man of great wisdom whose contribution I am sure, to the whole dominion-provincial discussions, was immeasurable. The viewpoint of Premier Robarts is not before us.
Premier Ross Thatcher of Saskatchewan had some questions to ask. He wrote the Prime Minister on August 21 and stated that he would appreciate it if the government could clarify the phrase: Contracting-out

Dominion-Provincial Relations provinces must continue to carry on programs of this nature. He also said that he would be very much interested in the amount of cash compensation to be paid in respect of the type C programs. There has been no letter tabled here representing the reply sent to the premier of Saskatchewan. There is nothing before us of any kind from the premier of Alberta. There is no definitive answer from any premier, except the premier of Quebec, and, I think I can say, also the premier of New Brunswick. I see no letter from the most important premier of them all, the premier of Prince Edward Island, where confederation began.
I am surprised that, since these discussions took place originally in June, and since the Prime Minister's letters were written in August, there has been no follow-up or further discussion in respect of this matter. These matters were discussed in June and the letters were written in August, yet down rings a curtain of silence over practically the whole subject.
I am concerned in this regard because there is no indication that the present dominion team is playing on its own side. It has often been the case throughout our history that the opposition in the dominion legislature has adopted strong provincial rights points of view. I think this is the first time in our history that a government on the dominion scene has become itself the champion of the provincial side of the argument. This will make history. I suppose it will be one of the great contributions that the present government will have made to our national development. However, if I were writing this speech instead of saying it I would put quotation marks around the word "great".
I must take to task my friend from the Northwest Territories. He was unfair to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). He referred to what the Minister of Finance had in mind for the maritimes. I believe he was unfair in not placing on the record the fact that, along with shipping us out to more lush parts of the country, the Minister of Finance was going to give us some travelling assistance. Whether this was to be in the form of first class tickets, or coach class tickets, or tourist class tickets, I do not know, but I think the record should be set straight. It was his suggestion that we should be subsidized in our move from the maritimes to more profitable areas.
Some of us have decided to remain in the maritimes. Some of us have found that staying there is a little easier and a little better
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
because there once was a government, not too long out of office-although it seems a long time-which looked upon this whole question differently. That government had some conception and appreciation of national goals as well as provincial needs.
It is easy to say that certain provinces can carry out programs of social welfare and development, and possibly there are provinces which are able to do so and can do so very well. It is natural that we must look at the jurisdictional rights of provinces as well as the economic needs. However, there is something which must never be forgotten in respect of this whole area, and that is the economic inequity which exists among the provinces.
Confederation was many things, but one thing it was, was a sharing of economic advantages and disadvantages. One of the great accomplishments of the former government was its ability to look across this land and see that inequity had been allowed to continue and become more acute. It used the powers of the national government to redress some of the long standing wrongs, just as it looked at the various sectors of Canadian society, such as agriculture, and took steps to bring remedial measures to the fore.
It is all very well to talk about the rights of the provinces. We know that these areas are areas of provincial jurisdiction, but what would this country be without the initiative that has to be taken by national governments? One of the members who spoke in this debate the other day, the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton), was in large measure responsible for two of the finest programs that this country has ever seen, programs which have brought benefits to people from Halifax to Victoria. I refer to the roads to resources program and the ARDA program. There are many welfare and development programs which many of the provinces could never initiate. Are we to say that is too bad, there are provinces that can, so let the others enjoy their lower standard of income? Let them call on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) for a little travel assistance for their people to move to those areas where such programs may be carried out.
We are living in an age of mobility. Canadians move about more than ever before. We have recognized the principle of portability in pensions. Let us not lose sight of national needs and the inequalities that exist in various areas of the country.

I know that the burdens upon the provinces are great because in 1867 the provinces were given many areas of legislative responsibility which at that time were considered minor in economic terms. Welfare and highways were not very expensive in the 1860's. The great expenditure was on railways instead of highways and the dominion government had the responsibility for railways. But not long after confederation we entered the so-called welfare age and the expenditures over the years have become immense. In 1926-27 the federal government spent on welfare $49.7 million. In 1956 the amount had arisen to $1,402 million. I do not bring this forward for partisan reasons but when the government which I supported took office the amount was increased from $1,402 million to $2,575 million, the greatest increase of any like period in our confederation.
One thinks of the great benefits brought to many people. One thinks of those provinces which could not mount these programs on their own. Tonight I heard many speakers talk in general terms about the problems of the relationship between the great founding races of this country. Some say they are not separatists. I would go even farther than that and say that I am anti-separatist. We do not want any part of this country to leave. I should like to see French Canada take an ever-increasing part in the dominion government. I am one of those who is not French speaking but who will support their every legitimate claim to recognition within the dominion governmental apparatus. It was a shocking thing that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) had to make a complaint the other day, and the manner in which it was initially rebuffed was even more shocking. We want closer relationships, not a moving away but a closer drawing together.
I know it is quite proper constitutionally and juridically for any province to move into these areas. Many of them were theirs originally, but I wonder if it would not be a great piece of statesmanship, or are we expecting too much, to try to bring about a pooling together of national programs so that we would have more, not less. Things are moving very fast in the world today and the world is not moving in the direction of decentralization at all. There are many countries in the world which are of the opinion that a national entity is now too small and they must progress toward something larger. Is it wise for Canadians to move in the opposite direction? At moments of greatness, in moments of peril too, this country has found 20220-821
Dominion-Provincial Relations it necessary to look to Ottawa for leadership. We must make sure that at Ottawa all parts of this country are able to make their proper impact.
I could never welcome any move which would weaken the national structure. If we look back over the last two years, do we not see evidence of the weakening of the national structure? It is all very well to describe it in juridical and constitutional terms but if we have a shuffling off of the economic potency of the dominion government in the direction of regional ones, constituent ones, the provinces, surely the ability of the central government to redress economic wrongs and to provide equalization or an approach to equalization has been diminished at a time when our needs are great.
Like many other speakers who have taken the issue beyond the constitutional and the economic, in my opinion we are struggling in Canada, as we often are, to find a national expression. We are worried about the parts breaking away, and it is one of the unfortunate elements of our day that we have on the national scene one of the weakest governments since confederation. I say this not with partisan delight but with great sorrow, because now if ever is the time that we need a strong national government, a government with a sense of purpose, a government which the provinces could follow; but the provinces would have to know where they were going before any province would even get in line for any national purpose.
While I can say that I have seen a great many less desirable pieces of legislation than this one, like some of my colleagues I am concerned about the trend and the tendency, the acceleration toward decentralization that is reflected in the bill, proper as it may be constitutionally and legally. Obviously the legislation has been conceived after little discussion, but I wonder whether it is the kind of legislation which we should salute.
Therefore I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is a wise one. It would be nothing new for the government to have to reverse itself and have to change its mind. Everybody is doing it. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Nicholson) did it the other day, and in line with this perhaps we should look into this matter much more carefully and fully than we have. We should not enter into great constitutional changes without more study and having regard to the economic aspects it is this kind of study that the hon. member

Division
has recommended as wholesome and necessary at this time.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that is no answer at all. The interpretation I take from subclause 2 of clause 3 is that the supplementary agreement would have to contain exactly the same terms that are in the authorizing instrument or the agreements that are
20220-821J
Dominion-Provincial Relations in effect at the present time. If the provinces are going to be required to enter into a supplementary agreement, particularly with respect to hospitalization, that has exactly the same terms as the present agreement which runs until 1970, then it seems to me that Bill No. C-142 has no purpose whatever. If you interpret this exactly it seems that the provinces have no flexibility or latitude whatever to bring about a different kind of agreement. What purpose is there in transferring the authority for the administration of these programs if the provinces are going to be tied hard and fast to the authorizing instrument? This Bill No. C-142 is a farce if there is to be absolutely no change under the new agreements from the agreements that are in existence at the present time.
If you go farther you find in clause 9, subsections 1 and 2, that if the cost of operating any of the supplemental agreements is more than the province would receive in revenue from the percentage points of tax abatement, then the Minister of Finance is authorized to make a payment. On the other hand, according to subsection 2 of clause 9, if the yield from those percentage points of tax abatement is higher than the cost of the supplemental agreement, this then becomes a debt owing by the province to the federal government. So, what is the purpose of this bill? It seems to me it is an attempt to make it appear that the provinces have an additional degree of autonomy. If you put subclause 3 of subsection 2 together with clause 9 you find that there can be absolutely no change in the supplemental agreement from the agreements that are in effect at the present time. At the same time you find that they cannot have one dollar of extra money for the purpose of flexibility.
In other words, if they earn a dollar more than the programs cost it becomes a debt to the federal government. If the yield is less than the cost of the program, then the federal minister can make a grant. It seems to me we have come to that stage now in discussing Bill No. C-142 where we need some explanation as to where there is going to be any flexibility.

Dominion-Provincial Relations are now for this interim period. The only difference will be in the method of payment. This was a point which was quite clear to the hon. member for Edmonton West and quite clear to my hon. friend. It was less clear, apparently, to the hon. member for Yukon.
The bill is most definite that a supplemental agreement may only vary the terms of the original undertaking in two particulars, the manner in which Canada shall reimburse the provinces for their assumption of the former federal share of the cost and the manner in which the provinces shall keep the government of Canada informed as to provincial expenditures on the program. Now, that is fundamental to this bill. Some hon. members may disagree with it. Other hon. members, like the hon. member for Edmonton West, might say that this is not quite as world shattering as some people have led them to believe. As I have explained, this is an interim measure only. We will not get down to making basic changes until the tax structure committee has done its work and has reached a conclusion which it is prepared to bring to this house.

I have just a brief comment. I am glad to see the hon. member for Medicine Hat has followed very well the strictures I placed on this bill. It is obvious that Alberta is not going to get any relief in its dispute with the federal government in connection with the Alberta hospital insurance agreement. Now that Alberta has taken over the servicing of the capital cost of the hospital program, I understand the minister's officials are even disallowing the servicing cost of that part of the Alberta hospital insurance program. This is something less than they had before. One further point to show that this is a case of "plus ga change plus ga reste la meme chose". I suppose the situation is to be more or less unchanged because, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat pointed out, if the equalization formula proves insufficient under the operation of clause 9 a direct grant may be advanced provided the minister is satisfied, and so on. Well, he will be satisfied when he sees the operating costs after they have been announced. So there really will be no change, in practice.
My conclusion is that this bill is merely in response to the vanity of one provincial premier. There was an ultimatum, and this is the answer. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said the other day, the mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse. That is all this bill is-a mouse.

speechtext:
I should like to move that clause 3 be amended by deleting subclause
[Mr. Gordon. 1

(2). I do this because the provision of this subclause which ties a province to making a supplementary agreement which is completely in accordance with all the provisions which are now in the authorizing instrument is a clear contradiction in my view of all the promises which were made by the Prime Minister during the dominion-provincial conference on November 26, 1963. I am going to quote some of the statements that he made when talking to the provinces. This is what he said, according to the text, in his opening statement:
One can readily conceive of a new arrangement involving transfer to the provincial governments of full responsibility for some of the present cost-shared programs.
Then he said this:
One way to do this would be in the field of equalization payments and by increases in the abatements which the federal government makes in its tax laws to take account of provincial taxes.
There is no change. Under clause 9, if you consider both clauses 1 and 2, there is absolutely no change in the amount of money that a province can take from these 20 percentage points of tax abatement. If the supplementary agreement, as I said before, costs more than the yield from this abatement, then it becomes a debt by the province to the federal government; and on the other hand the federal government is authorized to make up the difference if the new agreement costs more than the yield from these abatements. So there is absolutely no transfer of responsibility for collecting tax, because when you reduce it to terms of absolute dollars in relation to the programs, it must remain exactly the same as in the so-called authorizing instrument. The premier of Ontario said this in his opening statement to the very same conference:
There...are defects in these conditional grants which should be remedied. The conditions attached to the grants are too rigid. They create administrative difficulties, fail to recognize fully regional needs and peculiarities, and often result in some services being overexpanded to the detriment of other services of higher provincial priority.
He went on to say this:
Every effort should be made to reduce the rigidities and to modify these arrangements so that federal interference in affairs of provincial responsibility is kept to a minimum.
By keeping subclause (2) in clause 3 there is absolutely no change that would give effect to these stated objectives of the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Ontario. The premier of Manitoba had this to say when he talked about the problems of joint
Dominion-Provincial Relations interest or responsibility in cost-shared programs:
It is precisely in these areas of mutual concern that we find what friction, disharmony and frustration perplex us today.
So, Mr. Chairman, as long as subclause (2) of clause 3 is in there, there is no real transfer of any authority either of the administration, the regulations or the details of the program; nor is there any transfer of any real authority in so far as tax collecting is concerned. It is for this reason that I move that we delete subclause (2) of clause 3.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order. Mr. Olson moves that clause 3 be amended by deleting therefrom subclause (2). I presume the hon. member means that the remaining clauses be renumbered accordingly.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Agreed.
Amendment (Mr. Olson) negatived: Yeas 5; nays 87.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. Shall clause 3 carry?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one other problem with clause 3 and that concerns the date. Subsection (3) of clause 3 says:
No supplementary agreement in respect of a standing program may be entered into after the 31st day of October, 1965-
It may be that there is no administrative difficulty here, but there may be one. For example, many of the legislative assemblies in the provinces are nearly ready to adjourn their 1965 session. If they do not provide during this current session of their legislature for the amount of income tax that they anticipate will be required in relation to any of the agreements into which they may enter, I am wondering what is going to happen between January 1, 1966 and the end of that fiscal year. Because I presume that the federal government would withdraw from the income tax field to that extent; and if that were done prior to the provinces having taken up the difference and passing an act to impose those percentage points of tax abatement, would the provinces be put in any difficulty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The provinces, of course, have copies of this bill, are fully familiar with it and have been for some time. They have probably decided what they want to do by

Dominion-Provincial Relations now, although they have not informed me to that effect. If a province should on October 31, 1965, enter into an agreement, and if the government of that province gave an undertaking to put forward legislation in their legislature changing their tax rates, I think that would be acceptable on the understanding that the changes would be retroactive, and if they were not, that there would be a satisfactory accounting.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can tell the Minister of Finance that there are some provinces who do not understand what is contained in Bill No. C-142. As a matter of fact they began studying it very recently since the Minister of Finance made his explanatory remarks on, I believe, March 17, which was the first time it came before the house for second reading, and they have begun to realize how inflexible supplementary agreements could be in relation to the old authorizing instruments. There are many provinces at the present time who have not decided out of which programs they are going to opt out.
For example, I know that my own province planned on opting out of some programs because the arrangements between the federal government and the province, so far as calculating the shares of the cost was concerned, were not satisfactory. However, after they studied the details, particularly of clause 3, a certain confusion and disappointment developed because the flexibility they expected to find was not in the bill.
I am sure there is a great deal of serious consideration taking place at this time in the cabinets of several of the provincial governments because Bill C-142 does not live up to the expectations they had. I am wondering whether it would not be the wise course to defer for six months the effective date of October 31, 1965. Many of the provincial authorities I am sure did not realize that this bill was as rigid as it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the second part of my explanation should be satisfactory. I cannot see that any province will not have had an ample opportunity to review the bill by October 31, 1965. I am sure most of the provincial authorities have already given consideration to this bill. The hon. member refers to the province of Alberta, and while it is true that the minister of health of that province was here a week ago and expressed certain disappointment because this bill did not do something which

it says it does not do, the words of the bill seem to be reasonably clear and there will be ample opportunity for a province to take advantage of the bill if it so desires.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, subclause 2 of clause 3 reads as follows:
A supplementary agreement shall contain an undertaking by the province that the province shall continue to operate the program in accordance with the authorizing instrument except as to the manner in which the government of Canada will contribute thereafter in respect of the program and the manner in which accounts are to be submitted.
Clause 3 is entitled "Standing programs" while subclause (2) deals with supplementary agreements. Does not the implementation of this clause involve for the federal government and for the provincial governments a duplication of expense and bureaucracy? In other words, a provincial bureaucracy controlling the federal bureaucracy and a federal bureaucracy watching what is going on in the province concerned.
We want explanations on that matter, that is, we want to know whether or not any province can administer its own program.
If a province decides to participate in a joint program or to work jointly with the federal government, will there be two organizations, two different administrations to be paid, one in the province and one in Ottawa, which would in fact double the administrative cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: If anything, I would think the effect of this would be to reduce the cost of supervision, and that sort of thing. The only thing the federal government will have to do before it pays out any money is to check and see that the money was spent for the purposes provided for in the act and under the agreement.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if there is any provision anywhere for changing the supplementary agreements. For example, at the present time the legislature of Alberta is considering changes in the administration of the hospitalization program to allow for the payment of some outpatient care. This is not in the authorizing instrument at the present time and I am wondering whether there is some provision for changing the supplementary agreements so that the cost of this outpatient care can be shared by the provincial and federal levels of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: It is hoped that such matters will be covered during the discussions of the tax structure committee. I should like to emphasize again that all provinces have expressed a very keen interest in and appreciation of this committee which was set up by them as well as by the federal government. It is hoped that all these points of difference and causes of irritation between the federal and provincial governments, such as there are in the case of several provinces including Alberta, will be discussed, but this particular bill does not provide for that kind of adjustment. Adjustments will be made after the tax structure committee has reached some agreement and it may well provide for a greater degree of flexibility than is contemplated here.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Then if the province of Alberta signed a supplementary agreement it would be necessary for the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Health and Welfare to come back to parliament for an amendment to this legislation before the federal government could participate in the payment of these outpatient costs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I have a question for the minister. Clause 3, subclause 1, refers to annex 1 and section 3(e) of annex 1 refers to student aid. However, there is a difference in terms between the French and English versions and I will refer to the French version.

Can the minister tell us whether the words "student aid" mean "school children aid"? What is the meaning of the word "student" in Schedule I?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: This clause refers to the university loan program.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: The French version and the English version may result in different interpretations because the word in French does not mean university students. It may mean a scholar or a lower grade student.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would let me have a look at the translation. If a correction is needed we will see that is done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Do I understand that clause 3 will stand?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may 1 say I will not disagree, provided the minister will
Dominion-Provincial Relations give us the assurance that the word "etudi-ant" means university students.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: That is intended.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Is it agreed that clause 3 will carry with this understanding?

Clauses 4 and 5 agreed to.
On clause 6-Increase of individual deduction from basic tax.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I have one question on clause 6. This tax abatement is for the term of a supplemental agreement only and if no further agreements were signed to carry out the terms of the supplemental agreement or the original agreement, I take it then the tax abatement would fall and there would be a reversion to the federal authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 7 agreed to.
On clause 8-Tax equalization payment.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I wonder if the Minister of Finance could perhaps lead us through the labyrinthian sentences in this clause and tell us what they mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
This is very simple, and I shall be glad to do so. The bill expresses the intent of the clause by declaring that the unit equalization value is the amount by which the per capita yield of a single unit abatement of the basic federal individual income tax in a province has to be increased in order that it will equal the per capita value-I am reading this slowly so my hon. friend can follow me-of a single abatement point in the two provinces in which the per capita value of a single abatement point is highest.
The tax equalization payment associated with each standing program is the value of the unit equalization in each appropriate province multiplied by the number of abatement units associated with the particular program. Now, I hope I have made myself clear, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I must compliment the minister on this masterpiece of clarity.
Clause agreed to.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
On clause 9-Payment to adjust for operating costs.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: First of all, I do not agree with clause 9, but it seems to be fruitless to move amendments. I believe subsection 2 should be deleted altogether so that a province could at least retain that part of the income tax that they will be able to levy. I should like to ask if the payments made by the federal government to provincial governments for their share of these programs will be paid on a monthly basis or a quarterly basis. Perhaps the minister could tell also when payments will be made for the equalization to adjust operating costs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the payments between the federal government and provincial governments now are very complex and are adjusted periodically. In the main, the payments will be made quarterly, to the best of my understanding.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: There is an important matter involved here. The cost of operating these programs has to be paid by the provinces until the federal government comes through with its share. If the federal government payment is delayed for several months it may become a rather heavy burden for some of the provinces to borrow the money and pay these month by month operating costs. I am wondering if the minister will not undertake to see that the provinces will not suffer a financial loss by way of having to pay bank charges and so on, if federal payments are delayed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I do not know how far I should go, Mr. Chairman, but within the limitations of the strictures imposed upon the government by interim supply and these other opportunities for reviewing expenditures by parliament, I would agree with him completely that payments should be prompt and provinces should not be imposed upon in the way he suggested. I should like to have an opportunity to review the practice at the moment before going further.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That is not a satisfactory answer-that the minister wants to review this. I think the provinces have a right to know from the minister, before they have to consider whether or not they want to enter into these supplementary agreements, when these payments are going to be made. If there is to be a hold-up it seems to me that the Minister of Finance could give an undertaking based on the federal share of these programs in the past, and work out arrangements by which regular interim payments
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).)
would be advanced at least to the extent of the federal share of these programs, so that the provincial governments would not be required to pay financing charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The practice is to make payments quarterly and to adjust at the end of the year. This has been the case since 1957.
I think the same practice should be continued, otherwise we would be in all sorts of difficulty. I should like to look into exactly what the practice is now, and perhaps I should make a statement on third reading.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: It would be agreeable to have a statement on third reading, but there are to be substantial changes in our practice. For example, we are transferring 20 points of tax abatement to the provinces which the provinces will have to levy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: May I answer that? All this means is that certain tax revenues which previously flowed into the federal treasury and which were then used to reimburse the provinces will go directly into the treasuries of the provinces. I am not in a position to say whether this means that any province will get a few dollars earlier or later than under the present system; I do not believe it will make any appreciable difference of any kind.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I presume the federal Minister of National Revenue will collect this income tax abatement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Only in some provinces, not in all.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: In nine out of ten.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: If the federal government is to collect these 20 percentage points of tax abatement and then turn the proceeds over to the provinces, when is this going to take place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: I have just received some expert information on this point which will probably make any further explanation on third reading unnecessary. The equalization payments will be made monthly and the estimated adjustments will be added or subtracted monthly.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That is very useful information, and I am sure the provinces will be pleased to hear that these payments will be made monthly.
One other question before we pass clause 9. It concerns the turning over of the 20 percentage points of income tax collected by the

federal government on behalf of the provincial governments. Will the total amount have to wait until all the income tax returns are in on April 30, or whenever they are due, or will there be interim payments in this respect, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: There will be interim payments adjusted monthly with a final adjustment later.
